SSRN and RePEc cover social science and economics working papers, which in economics circulate years before journal publication and are the current state of the field. The Directory of Open Access Journals, CORE, Semantic Scholar, and Unpaywall all help locate legitimately free copies. Authors will almost always send a copy if emailed politely, and library interlibrary loan remains a real and cheap option. Patents are a distinct and remarkable resource. A patent must disclose the invention sufficiently for a skilled practitioner to reproduce it, in exchange for a time-limited monopoly, usually twenty years from filing. That bargain means patents contain working technical detail that companies would otherwise treat as secret. Applications typically publish eighteen months after the priority filing date, which makes the corpus a leading indicator: a surge of filings in a technology area shows up well before products do. The free searchable systems include the United States Patent and Trademark Office's public search, Espacenet from the European Patent Office, PATENTSCOPE from the World Intellectual Property Organization, and Google Patents, which is the friendliest starting point and offers machine translation. Reading the assignee field maps who is investing in what, the citation network maps which prior work a field considers foundational, and the classification codes let you retrieve a whole technical area at once. Standards documents are the third leg. Bodies such as the International Organization for Standardization, the International Electrotechnical Commission, ASTM International, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, and the various national standards bodies define what a product must do to be sold or certified. Standards are frequently paid documents, often a few hundred dollars each, but the scope statements and tables of contents are public and the existence of a standard tells you a market has matured enough to need one. The date a standard was ratified is often the cleanest available marker for when a technology crossed from experimental to commercial, and revisions to it track how the field's consensus has moved since.

sections.heading: Trade Press, Industry Associations and Grey Literature
sections.body: Every industry of any size has a specialist press that the general public has never heard of, and it is frequently the fastest route to understanding how an industry actually works. These publications are written for practitioners by people embedded in the trade, which means they assume knowledge, name names, quote real prices, and report the operational detail that consumer media omits. A single afternoon reading the last eighteen months of a trade weekly will teach you more about a sector's cost structure, its consolidation pressures, and its live controversies than a stack of general business coverage. Trade titles also run annual rankings, capacity surveys, and buyers' guides that amount to free directories of who exists and how big they are. Industry associations are the natural companion. Associations exist to lobby and to serve members, and both missions generate data. They publish shipment statistics collected confidentially from members and aggregated, which is often the only measurement of a category's volume in existence; they publish member directories that function as a census of firms; they publish position papers that state the industry's own view of its threats. Association shipment data is usually good, because members have an interest in accurate benchmarks, but it covers members only, so the total will understate a fragmented market and the coverage ratio is the number you must ask about. Many associations sell their statistical yearbooks to non-members for a modest fee and give summary figures away in press releases. Grey literature is the librarian's term for everything published outside formal commercial or academic channels: consultancy white papers, conference presentations, think-tank reports, non-governmental organisation studies, government working papers, dissertations, and technical memoranda. Conference decks are especially valuable because speakers show operational numbers to peers that would never appear in a press release, and organisers often post the slides. Investor days and capital-markets days run by public companies produce the same effect at higher production values, complete with market maps, addressable-market estimates, and multi-year targets, all archived on the investor-relations section of the corporate website. The handling rule for all of this material is that it is unrefereed. Nobody checked it. A number in a trade magazine may be an association statistic, a company's own claim, an analyst's estimate, or a reporter's arithmetic, and the article will often not distinguish. Treat every figure as a pointer to a source rather than a source, and chase it one link back before you rely on it. When the chase dead-ends at a press release or at another article citing the first, you have learned that the number is unsupported, which is itself a useful finding. Keep such figures if you must, but label them clearly in your notes as claims rather than measurements, because six weeks later you will not remember which was which.

sections.heading: Digital Exhaust: Search, Traffic, Postings and Other Behavioural Traces
sections.body: A newer class of sources measures behaviour rather than outcomes, and it has transformed how quickly a market can be sketched. Search-interest indices report how often people query a term over time and by region. The important caveat, routinely ignored, is that such indices are normalised: a value of one hundred means the peak of the selected series in the selected window, not an absolute volume, so two separately-run charts cannot be compared and a flat line does not mean flat demand. Used correctly, search data is excellent for seasonality, for relative comparison between terms queried in the same chart, for geographic concentration, and for detecting the moment a term enters common use. Keyword planning tools attached to advertising platforms give bucketed absolute volumes and, more usefully, the price advertisers are willing to pay per click, which is a direct market signal of how valuable that intent is. Web-traffic estimation services model visits to a domain from panels and clickstream partnerships. Their absolute numbers are unreliable, sometimes off by a factor of two or more, particularly for smaller sites, but their relative rankings and trend shapes within a comparable set are usually sound. App-store intelligence firms model downloads and revenue the same way with the same caveats. Job-posting data is one of the strongest under-appreciated signals: aggregated postings reveal which capabilities a company is building before it announces anything, and counting engineering postings by specialism across a peer group maps strategic direction with unusual clarity. Reviews and ratings counts on marketplaces provide a crude but consistent proxy for cumulative unit sales within a single platform, since the review rate for a category tends to be stable even though its absolute level is unknown. Physical-world traces are increasingly accessible too. Bills of lading for seaborne trade are public records in several jurisdictions and are aggregated commercially, letting you see which importer received how many containers from which supplier. Ship and aircraft transponder feeds show movements. Satellite imagery, now sold at moderate prices, is used to count cars in retail car parks and to measure stockpiles and construction progress. Corporate website archives held by the Internet Archive let you reconstruct a company's price list or product range at any past date, which is often the only way to establish what something used to cost. The discipline these sources demand is calibration. Each of them is a proxy with an unknown and drifting multiplier between what it counts and what you care about. The professional move is to anchor the proxy against one known point. If you can establish from an audited filing that a company sold a certain number of units in a year, and you know its review count or traffic in that same year, you have a ratio you can apply cautiously across comparable firms, with the ratio's uncertainty carried forward honestly.

sections.heading: Evaluating a Source: Provenance, Method, Incentive and Age
sections.body: Every number you keep should survive four questions, and asking them takes about ninety seconds once the habit is formed. Who originally produced this, by what method, with what reason to want a particular answer, and as of when. Provenance means tracing the number to the body that actually did the measuring, not the outlet that repeated it. Aggregator sites and news articles are indexes, not sources, and the good ones say so explicitly by naming their origin. If you cannot reach an originating organisation with a stated methodology in two or three hops, the number is folklore. This matters more than it sounds, because the same figure can circulate through dozens of outlets and acquire authority purely from repetition. Method means how the observation was made. For a survey, the questions are sample size, how respondents were recruited, the response rate, how the results were weighted to the population, the exact wording of the question, and the margin of error. A thousand-respondent national survey carries a sampling margin of roughly plus or minus three percentage points at ninety-five per cent confidence for a proportion near fifty per cent, and that margin applies only to sampling error, not to the far larger errors introduced by a biased panel or a leading question. For a market size, the question is whether the figure was built from the bottom up by counting units and prices, or from the top down by taking a larger total and applying a share assumption. Bottom-up figures are usually more defensible; top-down figures inherit every error in the assumption. For a forecast, the question is what mechanism drives the growth rate, and if the answer is that the analyst extrapolated the last three years, you should say so in your own write-up. Incentive means asking who paid and what they sell. This is not an accusation of dishonesty; it is a recognition that funders shape questions. A study of a market's size commissioned by the largest vendor in it will use a definition that is generous to that vendor's product scope. A trade association's estimate of its industry's economic contribution will count indirect and induced effects that a neutral economist would treat sceptically. An advocacy organisation will select the true statistics that favour its case. Funding disclosure is normal in academic work and should be looked for; in commercial work its absence is the norm and you must infer. Age means both the reference period and the publication date, which are different and frequently confused. A report published this quarter may rest on a survey fielded two years ago against a base year three years before that. Write down the reference period, not the publication date, in your notes. In fast-moving categories a three-year-old figure is not evidence about today; it is history, and should be presented as such.

sections.heading: Reading a Market-Size Number: Addressable, Served and Obtainable
sections.body: Most published market sizes are quoted without saying which of several quite different quantities is being measured, and a great deal of confusion dissolves once the layers are separated. The widest layer is the total addressable market, the annual revenue that would be earned if every conceivable buyer bought the product from somebody. Inside that sits the serviceable available market, the portion reachable given real constraints of geography, regulation, language, channel, and product fit. Inside that again sits the serviceable obtainable market, the share a specific firm could plausibly win over a defined period given competition and its own capacity. These three numbers commonly differ by one or two orders of magnitude. A business plan that quotes the widest figure and implies the narrowest is not lying about arithmetic; it is lying about which question it answered. Several further distinctions decide whether two figures are even comparable. Revenue at manufacturer level, at wholesale level, and at retail level differ by the whole distribution margin, which in consumer goods routinely doubles the number between factory gate and shelf. Units and value move independently: a category can grow ten per cent in units while shrinking in value if prices are falling, which is exactly what happened across consumer electronics for decades. Installed base is a stock, annual sales are a flow, and treating one as the other is a classic error. Gross merchandise value, the total value of goods transacted through a marketplace, is not revenue to that marketplace, which earns only a commission, and conflating the two has produced some spectacular valuation mistakes. Nominal figures include inflation and real figures do not, so a market growing at four per cent nominally in a year of four per cent inflation has not grown at all. Currency and geography need explicit handling. A global figure converted at current exchange rates will swing with the currency market independently of any change in underlying activity, which is why serious comparisons over time are often made at constant exchange rates or at purchasing power parity. Whether a regional figure includes or excludes a large adjacent country changes it materially, and definitions of regions differ between research houses. Finally, treat compound annual growth rates with suspicion proportional to their length. A rate quoted over eight or ten years smooths away every interesting feature of the path, and it is arithmetically dominated by the endpoints, so choosing a trough as the base year manufactures an impressive number. Ask what the year-by-year series looks like. If the source will not provide it, the growth rate is a marketing claim. When you write up a market size yourself, state the layer, the price level, the units, the currency, the base year, and the geography in the same sentence as the number. It is four extra clauses and it makes the figure usable by someone who was not in the room.

sections.heading: Triangulation: Building an Estimate That Survives Scrutiny
sections.body: Triangulation means constructing the same quantity by two or more genuinely independent routes and comparing the answers. It is the closest thing secondary research has to an experiment, because independent methods do not share errors, so agreement is meaningful and disagreement localises the problem. The standard pairing is one top-down and one bottom-up estimate. A top-down estimate starts from a large, well-measured total and narrows it by a chain of shares. Suppose you want the annual spend on professional knife sharpening in a country of forty million people. You might start from a national household expenditure survey showing average annual household spend on personal and household services, take the number of households, and apply a share for the relevant sub-category. Every link in that chain multiplies uncertainty, so a top-down estimate with four assumed shares of plus or minus thirty per cent each has an honest range of roughly a factor of three either way. A bottom-up estimate counts the units. For the same question you might take the establishment count for the relevant industry code from official business statistics, say two thousand four hundred businesses, multiply by an average revenue per establishment derived from the same source or from filed accounts, say one hundred and forty thousand in local currency, and reach roughly three hundred and thirty-six million. Alternatively you might work from the consumer side: an estimated twelve per cent of households using the service once a year at an average ticket of thirty gives four point eight million households times thirty, or one hundred and forty-four million, which is a long way from the first figure and tells you immediately that either commercial and trade customers dominate, or one of your two inputs is badly wrong. That gap is the point of the exercise. Reconciling it is where the real understanding is produced. In this case the resolution is almost certainly that restaurants, butchers, and industrial users account for most of the revenue while households account for most of the transactions, which is a genuine structural insight you would not have reached from either number alone. Discipline the process by writing the estimate as an explicit chain with every assumption named, its source cited, and a plausible low and high value attached. Build it in a spreadsheet where each assumption is its own labelled cell rather than buried in a formula, so that a reader can change one input and see the consequence. Then run a sanity check against something you know independently: implied revenue per capita, implied share of household income, implied number of employees against the official employment count for the industry, or implied units against a physical constraint such as manufacturing capacity. Estimates that survive a per-capita and an employment check are rarely wildly wrong. Estimates that fail one and are published anyway are how a market comes to be described as larger than the total consumer spending of the country it is in, which happens more often than it should.

sections.heading: A Working Procedure for a Secondary Research Sprint
sections.body: Unstructured searching expands to fill whatever time is available and produces a folder of tabs rather than an answer. A timeboxed procedure with a written decision question at the front converts the same hours into a defensible conclusion. The version set out here fits comfortably into three to five working days for one analyst and scales down to a single day for a narrower question. The essential discipline is that the question is written before the searching starts and is not allowed to drift silently, because a question that quietly broadens is the most common reason a sprint produces nothing usable. Keep a running list of things you wanted to know and could not find; that list is the specification for any primary research that follows, and it is frequently the most valuable single output of the whole exercise.
steps: Write the decision the research must inform in one sentence, name who will act on it, and state what answer would change their mind. Pin this where you can see it and do not edit it without noticing that you have.

Decompose that decision into no more than six answerable factual questions, each phrased so that a specific number, date, list, or yes-or-no answer would resolve it. Vague questions produce vague reading.

Identify the industry classification codes and the standard vocabulary of the field, including the terms practitioners use rather than the terms outsiders use, because search results depend entirely on hitting the insider word.
Run the official-statistics pass first: the relevant national agency tables, the international bodies, and the trade statistics. Record the exact table identifiers and reference periods as you go.

Run the disclosure pass: annual reports and prospectuses for the five to ten largest identifiable players, reading the business description, the segment note, and the risk factors rather than only the headline financials.
Run the association and trade-press pass to establish structure, vocabulary, live disputes, and any shipment or capacity statistics the industry collects about itself.

Run the scholarly and patent pass if the question involves technology, cost trajectories, health claims, or anything where mechanism matters, and note the most-cited references the field keeps returning to.
Build the estimate twice, once top-down and once bottom-up, with every assumption in its own labelled spreadsheet cell, a cited source beside it, and a low and high value attached.
Reconcile the two estimates explicitly and in writing. Where they disagree by more than a factor of two, find the offending assumption before proceeding rather than averaging the results.
Sanity-check the answer against an independent constraint such as population, household income, industry employment, or physical capacity, and record the check so a reader can repeat it.

Write the finding as a short memorandum stating the number, its definition and boundaries, the confidence range, the two or three assumptions it is most sensitive to, and the open questions that remain.

sections.heading: What You Need to Work Efficiently
sections.body: Secondary research needs almost no equipment and a surprising amount of access, and the gap between a frustrating afternoon and a productive one is usually a matter of having arranged the access in advance rather than discovering the paywall at the moment of need. The items below are the practical kit, and most of them cost nothing beyond the effort of registering. The single highest-leverage item is a library affiliation, because research libraries collectively subscribe to most of the commercial material an individual could never justify buying, and many national and large municipal libraries grant remote database access to any resident with a card. Arrange that before you need it. The second highest-leverage item is unglamorous: a habit of saving rather than bookmarking. Links decay, paywalls descend on pages that were open last month, and statistical agencies retire old tables when a new vintage supersedes them. An analyst who kept the PDF can still defend a claim two years later; an analyst who kept the link often cannot. Nothing here requires a paid subscription to begin. A great deal of serious market work has been done with nothing but a national statistical portal, a securities filing system, a patent search, a library card, and a spreadsheet, and it is worth exhausting those before concluding that the answer must be bought. Reaching the limits of free material at least tells you precisely which question you are paying to answer.
ingredients: A public or academic library card with remote database access, which commonly unlocks industry report collections, newspaper archives, company directories, and academic journals at no cost to the reader.

Accounts on the free official portals for your geography: the national statistical agency, the securities regulator's filing system, the company registry, the patent office search, and the central bank's data service.

A reference manager or a plain structured note file that stores, for every fact kept, the originating organisation, the exact document title, the reference period, the publication date, the page or table number, and the retrieval date.
A spreadsheet discipline in which each assumption occupies its own labelled cell with a source note attached, so that the estimate can be re-run when one input changes.
Access to a web archive service for retrieving pages, price lists, and product ranges as they existed at a past date, since corporate sites are edited without notice.
A document reader that searches inside PDFs, because annual reports run to hundreds of pages and the useful paragraph is never in the summary.
Currency and inflation conversion tables from an official source, so that figures from different years and countries can be placed on a common basis rather than compared naively.
A written list of the industry classification codes relevant to your market, since these are the keys that unlock most official databases and are tedious to rediscover repeatedly.
Contact details for the relevant trade association and the editorial desk of the leading trade publication, both of which will often answer a polite factual question for free.

sections.heading: Building and Maintaining the Research File
sections.body: The difference between research that compounds and research that evaporates is the file. Most analysts discover this the hard way, six months after a project, when a colleague asks where a number came from and the honest answer is that it was in a tab that is now closed. A disciplined file costs perhaps five per cent extra effort at the time of reading and repays it many times over. The minimum record for every fact you intend to use has seven fields: the originating organisation, the exact document title, the specific location within it such as a table number or page, the reference period the data describes, the publication date, the retrieval date, and a stable link or file copy. The reference period and the publication date must be recorded separately because they routinely differ by years and conflating them is the single most common citation error in commercial work. The retrieval date matters because online sources are edited silently; a page that supported your claim in March may not in September. Keep a local copy of anything load-bearing, as a PDF or a saved page, because links rot at a rate studies have repeatedly measured in the range of several per cent per year and paywalls appear where none were. Alongside the citation, record two things that pure bibliographic tools omit. First, a one-line note on how the figure was produced, in your own words, so that a later reader knows whether it was measured, modelled, or asserted. Second, an explicit confidence tag. A simple three-level scheme is enough: measured, meaning an official or audited count; estimated, meaning a defensible model with stated assumptions; and claimed, meaning an unverified assertion by an interested party. Colour-coding a spreadsheet by these three tags immediately reveals whether a conclusion rests on evidence or on a stack of press releases, and that single visual is often more persuasive to a decision-maker than the analysis itself. Structure the file around questions rather than sources. A folder per source produces a filing cabinet; a document per question, with the competing evidence gathered under it and the disagreements written out, produces an argument. Where sources conflict, keep both and record the conflict explicitly with your reasoning about which you favour and why, rather than quietly dropping the inconvenient one. That habit protects you when the inconvenient source later turns out to be right. Finally, date the whole analysis prominently and state its shelf life. A market sizing built on a base year is a photograph, not a live feed. Writing on the front page that the figures are as of a stated quarter and should be refreshed when the next official release lands prevents the document from being quoted as current three years later, which is the fate of most unmarked research.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and How Estimates Go Wrong
sections.body: Certain failures recur so reliably across industries and decades that they are worth learning by name, because recognising the pattern is most of the defence. The first and most damaging is circular citation. A number appears in a press release, is repeated by a trade publication, is cited from that publication by a consultancy, is quoted from the consultancy by a newspaper, and now appears in four independent-looking places. Analysts count the four mentions as corroboration when in fact there is one unsupported source. The defence is mechanical: chase every important figure back until you reach an organisation that describes how it measured, and if the trail loops or dead-ends, mark the number as unsupported. Doing this once or twice on a familiar statistic is a bracing education, because a surprising share of widely-quoted market figures collapse under the first pull. The second is definitional drift. A series is compared across years or countries when the underlying definition changed. Industry classifications are revised every few years and codes are split, merged, and renumbered; survey questions get reworded; a statistical agency changes its treatment of a category. The resulting step change in the data looks like a real event and gets explained as one. The defence is to read the revision notes before drawing any multi-year chart. The third is survivorship and coverage bias. Directories, association memberships, review platforms, and funding databases all systematically over-represent firms that still exist, are large enough to be noticed, and have a reason to be listed. Average revenue computed across a directory therefore overstates the true average across all firms, sometimes badly. The defence is to ask what the denominator would have to be for the sample to be representative, and to check it against an official establishment count. The fourth is false precision. A figure assembled from four assumptions each uncertain by a third is quoted to three significant figures because that is what the spreadsheet displayed. This is not a cosmetic problem; precision signals confidence, and downstream readers make decisions on the implied confidence. Round to the precision the weakest input supports, usually one or two significant figures, and quote a range. The fifth is the forecast that is really an extrapolation, presented with a compound growth rate and no mechanism. When a projection cannot name what physically or economically produces the growth, treat it as a scenario rather than a prediction. The sixth is stale anchoring, where an old figure becomes the accepted baseline and later work adjusts from it rather than rebuilding. When you inherit a number, find out how old its foundation is before you build on it, because inherited anchors have been known to persist unchallenged through a decade of successive reports.

sections.heading: Legal, Licensing and Ethical Limits
sections.body: Secondary research operates inside a legal frame that varies by jurisdiction and is genuinely unsettled in places. What follows is orientation, not legal advice, and anything with commercial consequence deserves a lawyer who knows your jurisdiction. The foundational principle in United States law is that facts themselves are not copyrightable. The Supreme Court settled this in Feist Publications versus Rural Telephone Service in 1991, rejecting the older sweat-of-the-brow doctrine and holding that a telephone directory's alphabetical listings lacked the minimal creativity copyright requires. You may therefore extract and restate factual information from a source in your own words. What is protected is the expression: the prose, the charts as drawn, the selection and arrangement where those reflect creative judgement. Reproducing a report's tables and figures wholesale, or quoting at length, is infringement regardless of attribution. The European Union takes a materially different line through the sui generis database right created by Directive 96/9/EC, which protects substantial investment in obtaining, verifying, or presenting a database's contents for fifteen years independently of copyright, so extraction of a substantial part of a European database can be unlawful even when the contents are bare facts. Licences layer contract on top of copyright and usually bind more tightly. Subscription research agreements routinely restrict circulation to named users, forbid redistribution outside the contracting entity, and prohibit quoting figures in materials shown to third parties without a separately purchased reprint licence. Violating these is a contract breach, and vendors do audit and enforce. If a number from a paid report will appear in an investor deck or a public document, read the licence clause on external use before you paste it. Website terms of service similarly govern automated collection. The legal position on scraping publicly accessible pages has moved in the United States toward treating terms-of-service breach as a contract matter rather than a computer-intrusion crime, following litigation between hiQ Labs and LinkedIn in the Ninth Circuit and the Supreme Court's narrowing of the relevant statute in Van Buren versus United States in 2021, but this is not a licence to scrape freely: contract claims, copyright, database rights, and trespass theories all remain live, and the position differs elsewhere. Personal data adds another regime entirely. Where information identifies living individuals, the European General Data Protection Regulation and comparable laws in other jurisdictions impose obligations regardless of whether the data was publicly posted. Aggregate market research rarely needs personal data, and the cleanest posture is to avoid collecting it. Ethically, the standards that matter most are attribution, honesty about confidence, and not laundering a competitor's confidential material through an intermediary because it arrived in your inbox. If you would be uncomfortable explaining in public how you obtained a figure, that discomfort is the relevant signal.

guides.title: Customer Discovery Interviews
guides.summary: A complete practical method for interviewing potential customers to find out whether a problem is real before building anything: how to recruit, what to ask, how to avoid the biases that make interviews lie, and how to turn transcripts into decisions.

sections.heading: What Customer Discovery Is and Why Most Products Fail Without It
sections.body: Customer discovery is the practice of talking to potential users about their existing lives and problems, before and instead of pitching them something, in order to find out whether the problem you intend to solve is real, painful, and worth paying to remove. It is deliberately not sales, not market research in the survey sense, and not usability testing. Its output is not a purchase order and not a satisfaction score; it is a corrected understanding of who has the problem, how they currently cope, and what it costs them. The reason it matters is blunt. Post-mortem surveys of failed startups conducted by CB Insights have repeatedly found that the single most common self-reported cause of failure, cited in roughly a third to forty per cent of cases, is building something nobody wanted, ahead of running out of cash and being outcompeted. Those failures rarely involve bad engineering. They involve teams who built a good answer to a question nobody was asking, and who found out only after spending twelve to thirty months and their entire runway. The asymmetry is the whole argument for the practice: twenty conversations cost a few weeks of one person's calendar and no capital, while the alternative way of learning the same thing costs a company. The intellectual lineage runs through Steve Blank, who formulated customer development in his 2005 book The Four Steps to the Epiphany after a career of expensive failures, and whose central slogan is that there are no facts inside the building. Eric Ries built the Lean Startup framework around it in 2011, adding the validated-learning and build-measure-learn vocabulary. Rob Fitzpatrick's short 2013 book The Mom Test contributed the most useful tactical correction, which is that the problem with interviews is not that people lie but that the questions invite them to. Clayton Christensen's jobs-to-be-done framing, and Bob Moesta's associated switch interview technique, supplied the most useful analytical lens for what to listen for. A few distinctions are worth fixing early because confusing them wastes whole projects. Discovery is about the problem; validation is about whether your specific solution addresses it; usability testing is about whether people can operate what you built. Running them out of order produces confident nonsense, because a person who cannot operate your prototype will tell you about buttons when the real finding should have been that they had no reason to open the product at all. Discovery is also not a phase you complete. Mature companies run it continuously, because customers, competitors, and the jobs people are trying to get done all move. The habit worth building is a standing cadence of a few conversations a week, not a heroic burst of forty interviews before a launch and then silence for two years.

sections.heading: The Mom Test: Why Interviews Lie and How to Stop Them
sections.body: The foundational failure mode of customer interviews is that ordinary human politeness systematically corrupts the data, and it does so in a direction that always flatters the interviewer. People do not want to hurt your feelings. They are agreeable, they are imaginative about hypothetical futures, and they are unreliable narrators of their own future behaviour. Ask someone whether they would use an app that helped them cook healthier meals and a large majority will say yes, sincerely, and then never do it. The prediction is not a lie; it is a genuinely held belief about a hypothetical self that does not exist. Rob Fitzpatrick's rule of thumb, from which his book takes its name, is that a good question is one your own mother could not lie to you about even if she wanted to spare your feelings. That rule resolves into three concrete disciplines. First, talk about the person's life instead of your idea. The moment you describe what you are building, you have contaminated everything that follows, because the interviewee now knows what answer would please you. Second, ask about specifics in the past rather than generics in the future. The past is a fact that can be checked; the future is a guess dressed as data. Third, listen more than you talk, and treat compliments as noise rather than signal. The practical translation is a set of substitutions you should be able to make without thinking. Instead of asking whether someone would pay for a thing, ask what they currently pay for and what budget line it came out of. Instead of asking whether a problem is annoying, ask when it last happened, what they did about it, and how long it took. Instead of asking whether a feature sounds useful, ask them to walk you through the last time they needed it and what they did instead. Instead of asking what they want, ask what they have already tried, because attempted solutions are the most reliable evidence that a problem is real. Three categories of response should be mentally discarded rather than recorded as findings. Compliments carry no information; that sounds great and I love this idea tell you only that the person is polite. Generic statements such as I usually do things this way describe an idealised self rather than actual behaviour. Statements of future intent, including anything beginning with I would definitely, are near-worthless, because commitment made in a conversation costs nothing. The only future-facing signals worth anything are ones that carry real cost: a scheduled follow-up meeting, an introduction to a colleague or budget-holder, a deposit, a letter of intent, or permission to observe their process. Fitzpatrick calls these currencies of time, reputation, and money, and they are the only reliable answer to the question of whether a stated interest is real.

sections.heading: Framing the Hypothesis and Choosing a Segment
sections.body: An interview without a hypothesis is a pleasant conversation that produces anecdotes. Before recruiting anyone, write down what you currently believe in a form specific enough to be wrong. A workable template is that a named group of people experiences a named problem in a named situation, and currently deals with it in a named way, at a cost you can estimate. For example: independent bookkeepers with between five and twenty small-business clients lose two to four hours at every month end reconciling bank feeds that miscategorise transactions, and currently fix it by hand in a spreadsheet. That statement contains four separately falsifiable claims, which is exactly what you want, because a single conversation can kill one of them cleanly. The most common early error is defining the segment too broadly. Small business owners is not a segment; it is a census category containing a plumber, a Michelin-starred restaurant, and a two-person software consultancy, whose problems have nothing in common. A useful segment is narrow enough that its members share a workflow, share vocabulary, and can be found in the same places. The test is whether you can name three specific individuals or one specific list where you would find them. If you cannot, the segment is still an abstraction. Narrow ruthlessly at the start; you can always widen later, and it is far easier to generalise from a segment you understand deeply than to find signal in a wide sample of shallow ones. Distinguish carefully between the user, the buyer, and the beneficiary, because in business contexts these are often three different people with conflicting incentives. A nurse may be the user of a scheduling system, a hospital administrator the buyer, and the patient the beneficiary. Interviewing only nurses will yield an accurate picture of the pain and a completely wrong picture of the purchasing decision. Plan to interview each role, and expect their accounts to conflict; the conflict itself is a finding. Finally, write down in advance what result would make you abandon or substantially change the idea. This is the single most valuable discipline in the whole method and the one most often skipped. If you cannot articulate what disconfirming evidence would look like, you will not recognise it when it arrives, and you will instead accumulate a folder of quotes that support what you already wanted to do. Something as simple as deciding in advance that fewer than half of interviewees describing the problem unprompted means the hypothesis is dead gives the exercise real teeth. Set that threshold before you hear a single answer, because setting it afterwards is not a threshold, it is a rationalisation. Keep the written hypothesis visible during synthesis, and date it, so that when it changes you can see exactly what evidence moved you and when. Teams that skip this routinely discover months later that their stated target customer drifted three times without anyone ever deciding to change it.

sections.heading: Recruiting: Finding People Who Will Actually Talk to You
sections.body: Recruiting is where most discovery efforts quietly die, not because people refuse but because the founder finds asking awkward and lets the calendar fill with other work. The awkwardness is largely self-inflicted and comes from framing the request as a sales approach. Reframed as asking an expert about their own work, response rates climb sharply. People enjoy talking about themselves and their frustrations to someone who is genuinely listening, and the request costs them little. Warm channels come first because they convert best. Your own network, and the second-degree network reachable by asking three people for two introductions each, will usually supply the first ten to fifteen conversations. The critical discipline is to move beyond friends fast, because friends are the worst possible interviewees: they know what you want to hear and are maximally motivated to supply it. Treat warm contacts as a way to practise the script and to obtain introductions, not as a sample. Cold channels take more work but produce better data. Go where the segment already congregates and complains: trade association meetings, industry conferences, professional subreddits and forums, Slack and Discord communities, LinkedIn groups, local meetups, review sites where people write long angry reviews of the incumbent tool. Reviews are underrated as a recruiting source because the author has self-identified as both a user and someone with an opinion. For physical or local businesses, going in person during their quiet hours works far better than email. For hard-to-reach professionals such as clinicians or senior executives, a paid research panel or a recruiting agency costs somewhere between fifty and several hundred units of currency per completed interview and is often worth it, though screening quality varies and panel participants can become professional respondents who tell researchers what researchers like to hear. On incentives, the honest position is that they help response rates and introduce a bias. A modest gift card of twenty-five to a hundred units for a thirty-minute call is standard in consumer research and rarely distorts answers about past behaviour, though it does attract people with more time than problem. In business-to-business contexts money is often less effective than offering to share a summary of what you learn across all your interviews, which is genuinely valuable to a practitioner and costs you nothing. Write the outreach message short and specific. Name who you are, name the specific problem area, state plainly that you are not selling anything, ask for a defined and small amount of time, and propose two concrete slots. Twenty minutes asked for is more likely to be granted than an hour, and conversations that are going well routinely run over anyway. Expect response rates of roughly five to fifteen per cent on genuine cold outreach and thirty to sixty per cent on warm introductions, so plan the funnel accordingly: to complete twenty interviews from cold email you should expect to send on the order of two hundred messages.

sections.heading: Structuring the Conversation: The Discovery Script
sections.body: A discovery interview should be semi-structured, meaning you carry a written guide of themes and questions but follow interesting threads wherever they go. A rigid questionnaire wastes the format's single advantage, which is the ability to ask why in real time. A completely unstructured chat produces twenty conversations that cannot be compared with one another. The workable middle is a one-page guide with five or six themes, two or three opening questions under each, and a short list of things you must not leave without learning. The arc of a good thirty-minute conversation runs roughly as follows. Spend the first two minutes setting the frame: who you are, that you are researching how people handle a particular kind of work, that there are no right answers, that you will not be pitching anything, that you would like to record for your own notes, and confirming they are comfortable. Spend the next five minutes on context, establishing their role, the size and shape of their operation, and how a typical week runs, which both relaxes them and gives you the frame to interpret everything else. Then spend the core fifteen to twenty minutes on problem exploration, anchored relentlessly in specific recent episodes. Reserve the last five minutes for what Fitzpatrick calls the commitment and advancement step, and for asking for referrals. The highest-yield question in the whole method is a variant of walk me through the last time that happened. It forces recall of a specific episode rather than a summary of an average, and specific episodes contain the details that summaries sand away: who else was involved, what tool they opened first, where they got stuck, how long it took, what they did when it failed. Follow it with how often does that happen, what did it cost you, and what did you do about it. The last of these is the workhorse, because the existence of a workaround is the strongest available evidence that a problem is genuinely painful. People do not build spreadsheets, hire assistants, or set phone reminders for problems they do not care about. Two other probes earn their place. Asking what else they tried and why they stopped surfaces the competitive landscape more honestly than any direct competitor question, because it reveals what the person actually evaluated rather than what the market map says. And asking what would have to be true for them to change how they do this reveals the switching barriers, which are usually the reason a technically superior product fails commercially. Keep your own idea out of the conversation entirely until the final few minutes, and even then introduce it as a question about whether such a thing would have helped in the specific episode they described rather than as a pitch.

sections.heading: Question Craft: Open, Neutral, and Grounded in the Past
sections.body: The wording of individual questions does more damage than any other single factor, and the damage is invisible because a badly worded question still produces a fluent answer. Four properties separate a question that yields information from one that manufactures agreement. The first is openness. A question answerable with yes or no gives you one bit of information and usually the wrong bit, because agreement is the socially easier answer. Does the current process frustrate you invites yes; tell me about the last time the process went wrong invites a story. Convert every closed question in your guide into a how, what, or when. Why is powerful but occasionally puts people on the defensive about their own choices, so what led you to do it that way is often a gentler route to the same information. The second is neutrality. A leading question embeds the answer in the premise. How frustrating is the current reconciliation process presupposes frustration and will be answered on a scale of frustration even by someone who is not frustrated. The neutral form is how do you handle reconciliation at the moment. Watch particularly for evaluative adjectives smuggled into a question, for questions that offer only positive response options, and for the tone and body language that lead just as effectively as words. Nodding enthusiastically while someone describes a problem teaches them that describing problems pleases you. The third is grounding in the past. Anything phrased as would you, will you, or do you think you might is a request for speculation. Human beings are consistently poor at predicting their own behaviour, a finding robust across decades of research on the intention-behaviour gap, and in consumer contexts the gap between stated purchase intent and actual purchase is routinely a factor of two to five. Replace every hypothetical with its historical equivalent. Would you pay for this becomes what do you currently spend on this problem. Would you use it weekly becomes how many times did you do this last month. The fourth is singularity. Double-barrelled questions such as how easy and how fast is the current process force the respondent to answer one and drop the other, and you will not know which. Ask one thing at a time. Finally, master silence. After a person finishes an answer, wait three to five full seconds before speaking. This feels excruciating and is the single cheapest technique in the entire discipline, because the most useful material almost always arrives in what people add to fill the pause. Journalists and police interviewers both rely on it. Resist the urge to fill the gap with a helpful suggestion, which is really the urge to hear your own hypothesis confirmed.

sections.heading: Jobs to Be Done and the Switch Interview
sections.body: Jobs-to-be-done is a way of framing what you are listening for, and it changes the interview from a hunt for feature requests into an investigation of motivation. The core claim, associated with Clayton Christensen and popularised through his milkshake example, is that people do not buy products; they hire them to make progress in a particular circumstance. The milkshake study, conducted for a fast-food chain, found that a large share of milkshake sales happened before nine in the morning to solo commuters, who were hiring the drink to make a boring drive less tedious and to stave off hunger until lunch without crumbs or a free hand. Its competitors were bananas, bagels, and boredom, not other milkshakes. No amount of asking customers how to improve the milkshake would have surfaced that, because the answer lay in the circumstance rather than the product. A job statement is written as a situation, a motivation, and a desired outcome: when I am driving to work alone with a long commute ahead, I want something that occupies me and holds off hunger, so that I arrive without being bored or distracted by an empty stomach. The value of writing it this way is that it is solution-agnostic and therefore stable. Products change; the job persists for decades. The switch interview, developed by Bob Moesta and Chris Spiek, is the associated technique and is the most rigorous interview format in this whole field. It is conducted only with people who have recently switched to or purchased something, ideally within the last sixty to ninety days while memory is fresh, and it reconstructs the entire decision timeline backwards from the purchase. The underlying model is a timeline with four moments: first thought, when the person first realised something might need to change; passive looking, when they noticed relevant options without urgency; active looking, when they started seriously evaluating; and the deciding moment, when something forced a choice. Between those moments sit triggering events, and identifying the trigger is the point of the exercise, because triggers are what marketing can actually target. Moesta also frames the decision as a contest of four forces. The push of the current situation and the pull of the new solution drive change; the anxiety about the new solution and the habit of the present hold it back. Change happens only when the first pair exceeds the second. This is more useful than it sounds, because most teams work only on the pull, making their product more attractive, when the binding constraint is usually anxiety or habit. If interviews reveal that people love your category but never switch because migrating their data terrifies them, the correct product decision is a migration tool, not another feature. Ask specifically what almost stopped them, what they worried about, and what they had to give up, because those answers map directly onto the two restraining forces and are the ones teams almost never collect.

sections.heading: Running the Interview: Logistics and Procedure
sections.body: The mechanics matter more than they appear, because a badly run session loses data that no amount of analytical skill recovers. Two people is the ideal team: one interviewer who does all the talking and holds the relationship, and one note-taker who says almost nothing and captures verbatim quotes. Solo interviewing is workable but split attention costs you follow-up questions. Three or more people on your side turns a conversation into a panel and makes the interviewee guarded. Record whenever you have permission, and ask for it explicitly at the start rather than burying it in a form. Recording frees the interviewer from note-taking and preserves the exact wording, which matters enormously because customers' own phrasing is the raw material of later positioning and copy. Transcription is now cheap and near-instant, so the old objection that recordings are never reviewed no longer holds. Where recording is refused, respect it immediately and without negotiation, and write up from memory within fifteen minutes while recall is still accurate. In-person is richest because you see the environment and the body language, video call is a good second, and telephone loses enough that it should be a fallback. Best of all, where the work is observable, is asking to watch someone actually do the task, since the gap between how people describe their process and how they perform it is routinely large.
ingredients: A one-page interview guide with five or six themes and your must-learn list
A recording device or call-recording tool, plus a transcription service
A second person to take notes, ideally someone who will build the product
A shared document or spreadsheet with one row per interview for later synthesis
A pre-written consent line covering recording, storage, and anonymity
steps: Confirm the appointment the day before and restate that this is research, not a sales call.
Open by introducing yourself, explaining the topic in one sentence, stating there are no wrong answers, and asking permission to record.
Spend five minutes on context: their role, their scale, and what a normal week looks like.
Move to a specific recent episode with a phrase such as walk me through the last time you had to do this, then stay in that episode.
For each pain mentioned, ask how often it happens, what it costs, and what they did about it.
Probe alternatives already tried and why each was abandoned; note the exact words they use.
Resist describing your solution until the final five minutes, and only as a question about the episode they described.
Close by asking for a commitment that costs something real, such as a follow-up session, an introduction, or permission to observe.
Ask who else deals with this problem that you should speak to, and ask for the introduction there and then.
Write up within thirty minutes while the impressions are fresh, separating quotes from your interpretations.

sections.heading: Reading the Signal: Pain, Workarounds, and Commitment
sections.body: Not all findings are equal, and the central analytical skill is grading the evidence rather than collecting it. A useful mental hierarchy runs from weakest to strongest as follows: expressed opinion about a hypothetical, reported general behaviour, a specific recounted episode, an observed behaviour, an existing workaround, money already being spent, and finally a commitment made during your conversation that costs the person something. Treat anything in the first two tiers as background colour. Workarounds are the single most reliable signal available, and hunting for them should be a conscious objective of every interview. A workaround is any effort a person has already expended to reduce a pain: a spreadsheet built by hand, a recurring calendar reminder, a checklist taped to a monitor, a part-time assistant hired, two tools stitched together with copy-paste, a WhatsApp group serving as a ticketing system. Each one is a person spending scarce time or money on the problem without being asked, which is behavioural evidence that survives every politeness bias in the book. When someone shows you their spreadsheet, ask to see it, ask how long it took to build, and ask what breaks about it. That artefact is worth more than an hour of opinions. Quantify the pain wherever the person can help you. Hours per week, error rates, money spent, customers lost, deadlines missed. Numbers matter less for accuracy than for calibration: a problem costing someone twenty minutes a month is real but will not support a purchase, whereas one costing eight hours a month with a visible failure consequence probably will. A rough rule used by many business-to-business teams is that a solution must save or make roughly three to ten times its price to overcome purchasing inertia, so a tool priced at a hundred a month needs to be defensibly worth several hundred. Emotional intensity is a genuine but easily overread signal. Watch for spontaneous swearing, for the person leaning in, for unprompted repetition of the same complaint across the conversation, and especially for the moment they interrupt you to keep talking about it. Those are good signs. Politeness and mild agreement are not. The strongest signal of all is advancement, meaning that the relationship moves forward at real cost to them. Someone who books a second meeting, forwards you to their finance director, agrees to a paid pilot, sends you their actual data, or asks when they can have it, has spent time, reputation, or money. Someone who says this is fantastic, keep me posted, has spent nothing, and the correct interpretation of keep me posted is a polite no. Track advancement explicitly in your notes for every conversation; the ratio of advancements to interviews is a far better health metric than the ratio of enthusiastic responses.

sections.heading: The Biases That Corrupt Discovery, and Their Countermeasures
sections.body: Interview data is unusually vulnerable to bias because both parties are motivated to produce a pleasant conversation, and because the person analysing the data is the person who wants the answer to come out a particular way. Knowing the named biases is not sufficient; each needs a specific procedural countermeasure, because knowing about a bias does not protect you from it. Confirmation bias is the largest threat. Having formed a hypothesis, you will notice supporting quotes, ask follow-up questions that develop them, and mentally file contradictions as misunderstandings. The countermeasures are structural: write your kill criteria before you start, have a second person who did not originate the idea take notes, and deliberately spend part of each synthesis session listing evidence against the hypothesis before listing evidence for it. Social desirability bias makes people report what reflects well on them, which systematically distorts anything touching money, health, competence, or effort. People overstate how often they exercise and how carefully they read contracts, and understate how much they improvise. The countermeasure is to normalise the undesirable answer inside the question, for instance by asking how people usually end up handling this when things get busy, which gives permission for the messy truth. Acquiescence bias is the general tendency to agree, and it is stronger in some cultures than others and stronger when the interviewer holds higher apparent status. It is why yes-or-no questions are so damaging. The countermeasure is open questions and occasionally asking the same thing from the opposite direction to see if the answer flips. Selection bias operates at the recruiting stage and is the one most often invisible in the final report. If you recruited from a forum for enthusiasts of a category, you have learned about enthusiasts. If your first twenty interviewees came through your own network, you have learned about people demographically and professionally similar to you. The countermeasure is to record how each person was sourced and to check at synthesis whether findings differ by channel. Survivorship bias is the quiet killer in switch interviews: talking only to people who bought something tells you nothing about the far larger group who considered and declined, and the declines usually contain the more actionable information. Deliberately recruit people who evaluated the category and did nothing. Finally, recall bias degrades everything based on memory, with detail decaying sharply after a few weeks. This is the mechanical reason for anchoring on recent specific episodes and for the switch interview's sixty-to-ninety-day window. When someone summarises rather than recalls, they are reconstructing from a general belief, and you are now interviewing their self-perception. A blunt but effective habit is to end each synthesis session by writing one sentence naming the single strongest piece of evidence against the plan you are most attached to. If you cannot find one across twenty interviews, the most probable explanation is not that the idea is unusually sound but that you never asked a question capable of producing a no.

sections.heading: Synthesis: Turning Transcripts Into Patterns
sections.body: Twenty transcripts is a pile of anecdotes until it is processed, and the processing step is where most teams stop, which is why so many discovery efforts end with a vague sense that it went well. Synthesis is a distinct activity that needs its own scheduled time, ideally in a session of two to three hours with everyone who conducted interviews present. The standard method borrows from qualitative research and is straightforward. Begin by extracting observations onto individual cards or rows, one observation per card, each in the interviewee's own words where possible and tagged with who said it. An observation is something they said or did, not your inference about it. Keeping the two apart is the discipline that makes the rest work, because a note reading users want better search is an inference, whereas she opened three browser tabs and used the browser's own find function to locate the invoice is an observation, and only the second can be re-interpreted later when your understanding changes. Then cluster. Spread the cards out physically or in a shared board and group them by similarity without predetermined categories, letting the groups emerge and naming them afterwards. This bottom-up grouping is often called an affinity diagram and was formalised in Japan by Jiro Kawakita in the 1960s. The naming step is where the insight happens: forcing yourself to write a sentence that captures what a cluster of eleven quotes has in common produces sharper thinking than any amount of individual reading. Expect to regroup two or three times. Alongside the clusters, maintain a simple structured table with one row per interviewee and columns for segment, how they were sourced, the problem they described, its frequency, its cost, their current workaround, whether they had spent money, and what commitment they made. This table does the work that qualitative clustering cannot: it lets you count. If seventeen of twenty described the same problem unprompted, that is a finding. If four did and you built a compelling narrative from those four, that is a story you told yourself. Weight the evidence honestly when you write conclusions. Distinguish what most people said, what some said, and what one memorable person said, and never let vividness substitute for frequency. The single most articulate interviewee is dangerous precisely because their quotes are the most quotable. Finally, write the conclusions as claims with a confidence level and the evidence attached, and circulate them to everyone including the sceptics. A finding that cannot survive being read by someone who disagrees with the idea is not yet a finding. Keep the raw cards after the session rather than discarding them once the summary is written, because the next round of interviews will suggest new groupings, and re-clustering old observations under a better theory is often cheaper and more revealing than collecting fresh ones.

sections.heading: How Many Interviews, and When to Stop
sections.body: The most common question about discovery is how many interviews are enough, and the honest answer is that the number is set by a stopping rule rather than by a fixed target. The rule is saturation: you stop when additional interviews within a segment stop producing new information. In practice, teams find that the first five conversations upend everything, the next five refine it, and somewhere between the twelfth and twentieth the answers start sounding familiar and you can predict what the person will say before they say it. That predictive ability is the operational test of saturation. The empirical literature broadly supports this range. A widely cited 2006 study by Guest, Bunce, and Johnson analysing sixty interviews found that most themes appeared within the first twelve, and subsequent work has generally found saturation between nine and seventeen interviews for reasonably homogeneous groups. The important qualifier is homogeneity: saturation applies per segment, not across a study. If you are researching three distinct roles, you need saturation in each, so twelve to fifteen per segment, not twelve overall. Nielsen's much-quoted claim that five users find eighty-five per cent of problems belongs to usability testing, where the object is discrete defects in an interface, and it does not transfer to problem discovery, where the object is understanding a varied population's circumstances. Applying the five-user heuristic to discovery is one of the most common and most expensive misreadings in the field. A reasonable planning figure for a new problem space is fifteen to twenty-five conversations per segment for the initial pass, with the qualification that the first two or three are practice and should be treated as script debugging rather than data. If you reach twelve and the answers are wildly divergent, that is not a signal to keep going indefinitely; it usually means your segment is not really a segment and needs splitting. There are also two bad reasons to stop that deserve naming. The first is stopping because you got the answer you wanted, which is confirmation bias wearing a schedule as a disguise. The second is stopping because interviews are uncomfortable and building is fun, which is the most common reason in practice and is almost never stated aloud. A useful check is to ask whether the last three interviews changed your mind about anything at all. If they did, you are not saturated. If they did not, and you also cannot remember the last time any interview changed your mind, the more likely explanation is that you have stopped listening rather than that you have finished learning. One more practical caution: saturation is a property of the questions you asked, not of the market. A guide that never asks about budget will saturate quickly on budget, because it collects no variation there at all. Before declaring a segment understood, check that your must-learn list was actually covered in most conversations rather than quietly abandoned.

sections.heading: Business Buyers Versus Consumers: Two Different Games
sections.body: The same interview method applies in both contexts, but the shape of the problem differs enough that treating them identically produces predictable errors. In business-to-business discovery the decision is almost never made by one person. A typical purchase of any size involves an end user who feels the pain, a champion who advocates internally, an economic buyer who controls the budget, a technical or security evaluator with veto power, and often a procurement function whose incentive is to slow things down and extract discounts. Research by Gartner has repeatedly put the average buying group for a complex business purchase at somewhere between six and eleven people. The practical consequence is that a single enthusiastic user interview tells you almost nothing about whether the thing will sell. You must interview at least the user, the champion, and the economic buyer, and you must ask explicitly about the purchasing process: who signs, what the approval threshold is above which extra scrutiny kicks in, what the security review requires, when the budget cycle opens, and what happened the last time they bought something similar. That last question is the single most valuable in business discovery, because it maps the real process rather than the official one. Business interviews are also easier to get and richer per conversation. Professionals will happily give thirty minutes to discuss their own domain, and the problems are documented, quantifiable, and attached to budget lines. The cost quantification that is guesswork in consumer contexts is often precise here: they know what the manual process costs because someone is paid to do it. Consumer discovery inverts most of this. The decision is usually made by one person quickly, often emotionally, and often without conscious deliberation, which means people are poor explainers of their own consumer choices. Recruiting is harder because the incentive to help is weaker, so incentives and intercepts matter more. Stated willingness to pay is far less reliable than in business contexts, where a manager comparing a tool against a salary is doing genuine arithmetic. Habit, identity, and social context carry weight that they rarely carry in a procurement process, and they are exactly the factors people least accurately report. Two corrections follow. In consumer discovery, weight observation and behavioural evidence far more heavily than interviews alone, and get to a real test with real money as early as possible, because a landing page with a checkout button teaches you more about consumer willingness to pay than fifty conversations. In business discovery, weight the process mapping heavily, because the commonest business failure is not a product nobody wants but a product a user loves that no one can figure out how to buy.

sections.heading: Ethics, Consent, and Handling What People Tell You
sections.body: Discovery interviews collect personal information from people who are doing you a favour, and the obligations that follow are both ethical and, in most jurisdictions, legal. Treating this as paperwork to be minimised is a mistake, because a reputation for careless handling closes the door on a whole professional community very quickly. Informed consent means the person understands what the conversation is for, that participation is voluntary, that they may stop at any time or decline any question, what will be recorded, who will see it, and how long it will be kept. In an informal founder-led interview this can be delivered in three sentences at the start rather than a signed form, but it must actually be delivered. Recording without asking is not acceptable anywhere, and in several jurisdictions, including a number of United States states operating all-party consent rules, recording a call without every participant's permission is a criminal offence. Ask, get an audible yes on the recording itself, and move on. Data protection law applies to research data. Under the European Union and United Kingdom General Data Protection Regulation, interview recordings and notes containing names, employers, or identifying details are personal data, which brings obligations of lawful basis, purpose limitation, storage limitation, and the individual's rights of access and erasure. The proportionate practical response for a small team is to keep a short record of who was interviewed and when, store recordings in access-controlled storage rather than a personal laptop desktop, pseudonymise transcripts by replacing names with codes, delete recordings once transcribed unless you have a reason to keep them, and honour a deletion request promptly if one arrives. Where interviews touch health, finances, or other sensitive categories, the bar is higher and worth taking advice on. Confidentiality deserves particular care in business contexts, where an interviewee may tell you something their employer would not want shared. Do not repeat identifiable details to their competitors, do not use their company name in a pitch deck without written permission, and be wary of quoting anything that could identify them by inference even with the name removed, since a specific enough job description in a small industry is an identifier. Honesty about your purpose is the underlying obligation and the one most often bent. Telling someone you are doing research when you intend to sell to them is a small deception that poisons the data as well as the relationship, since the moment they sense a pitch, their answers become defensive. If you want to sell, sell openly. If you want to learn, learn openly. Finally, close the loop: send a short thank-you and, where you promised it, the summary of what you found. It costs ten minutes and it is the reason people take your second call.

sections.heading: From Findings to Decisions: Persevere, Pivot, or Stop
sections.body: Discovery is only worth the effort if it changes what you do, and the decision step is where the discipline most often collapses into a slide deck that everyone praises and nobody acts on. Force the findings into a decision with three possible outcomes. Persevere means the hypothesis survived: the segment is real, most of them described the problem unprompted, they have built workarounds, and several made a costly commitment. The correct next move is not to build the full product but to design the smallest test that could still prove you wrong about the solution, which is a different hypothesis from the problem one you have just tested. Concierge and Wizard-of-Oz approaches, where you deliver the outcome manually while pretending it is automated, are usually faster and more informative than a first version of software. Pivot means part of the hypothesis died and part survived, which is the most common and most valuable outcome. Blank and Ries catalogued the varieties, and it is worth knowing which one you are making. A customer-segment pivot keeps the problem and changes who has it, and is what happens when the pain turns out to be acute in an adjacent group you interviewed by accident. A problem pivot keeps the segment and changes the problem, and is what happens when interviewees kept redirecting you to something else that hurt more. A zoom-in pivot turns one feature into the whole product; a zoom-out does the reverse. Slack, Instagram, and YouTube are all famous zoom-in or segment pivots, and in each case the signal was there in how people actually used the earlier thing rather than in what they said about it. Stop means the evidence did not support the idea, and having a genuine willingness to reach this conclusion is what separates real discovery from theatre. Killing an idea after twenty conversations is a success, not a failure; it is the cheapest possible way to avoid a two-year mistake. The pre-committed kill criteria written before recruiting are what make this decision survivable, because they let the team retire an idea without anyone having to lose an argument. Whichever outcome you reach, write it down in a short document with the date, the hypothesis as originally stated, what was learned, what the decision is, and what would cause you to revisit it. This artefact costs an hour and pays for itself repeatedly, because six months later somebody will propose the abandoned idea again, and the record of why it was dropped, with the evidence attached, is what prevents relitigating it from scratch. Attach the strongest verbatim quotes; a customer's own sentence carries argumentative weight that a summary never does.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and How to Recover From Them
sections.body: Most discovery goes wrong in a small number of recognisable ways, and each has a specific remedy. The commonest is pitching instead of listening, which is nearly universal in first attempts because talking about your idea is enjoyable and asking about someone's boring workflow is not. The symptom is that your transcripts contain more of your words than theirs. The remedy is mechanical: measure your talk-time ratio from the recording and aim for under thirty per cent, and remove any description of your product from the first twenty-five minutes of the guide. The second is interviewing only friendly people, which produces uniformly encouraging results and no learning. The symptom is that nothing has surprised you. The remedy is to recruit from at least three unrelated channels and to deliberately seek out people you expect to disagree, including those who evaluated the category and chose to do nothing. The third is collecting feature requests. Interviewees, trying to be helpful, will design your product for you, and their suggestions are usually a poorly reasoned solution to a real problem they have not articulated. Treat every feature request as a clue and dig behind it with what would that let you do, and when did you last need that. Henry Ford probably never said the line about faster horses, but the underlying point stands: the request encodes the job, and the job is what you want. The fourth is the false positive from a single vivid interview, where one articulate person with an unusual situation reshapes the whole plan. The remedy is the counting table, which makes frequency visible and vividness irrelevant. The fifth is discovery theatre, where interviews are conducted after the roadmap is fixed in order to produce supporting quotes. This is worse than not doing discovery, because it launders a decision as evidence. The tell is that no interview has ever changed a plan.
