The only remedy is to run discovery before commitment and to publish the disconfirming findings alongside the supporting ones. The sixth is stopping after the initial burst. Discovery decays; a picture of your market accurate in one year is stale in the next. Teams that sustain it treat two to five conversations a week as a permanent obligation shared across product, engineering, and support, on the reasonable argument that a developer who has heard three customers describe a problem makes better decisions in thousands of small moments than one who has read a summary. Finally, if you conclude midway that your questions have been leading and your data is contaminated, the correct response is to fix the guide and rerun, not to salvage. Twelve clean interviews beat forty compromised ones, and the sunk cost of the bad ones is already sunk.

guides.title: Building a Minimum Viable Product
guides.summary: What a minimum viable product really is and how to build one: framing the riskiest assumptions, choosing an MVP type, running the test, reading the data honestly, and deciding whether to pivot, persevere, or stop.

sections.heading: The Idea in One Sentence
sections.body: A minimum viable product, universally shortened to MVP, is the smallest thing you can put in front of real customers that produces trustworthy evidence about whether your business idea works. Read that definition carefully, because every word is doing work and most failed MVPs die from misreading one of them. Minimum means stripped of everything not needed for the test, not merely small. Viable means a customer can actually get value from it or genuinely believe they will, not a broken demo. And product is, frankly, the misleading word: many of the best MVPs are not products at all but landing pages, spreadsheets, or a founder doing manually what software will someday do automatically. The purpose of an MVP is not to launch early, impress investors, or ship something fast for its own sake. The purpose is learning. Every new venture rests on guesses: that a particular group of people has a particular problem, that they want it solved badly enough to pay, that they can be reached at a sensible cost, that you can deliver the solution economically. Most of these guesses are wrong most of the time. Industry studies and venture-capital post-mortems consistently find that the leading cause of startup death is not bad engineering or running out of money as such, but building something nobody wants; the analytics firm CB Insights has for years placed "no market need" at or near the top of its recurring analysis of startup failure reasons. The MVP is the discipline that attacks this risk first. Instead of spending a year and your savings building the full vision and then discovering the market's verdict, you spend weeks building the smallest credible probe and let reality vote early, while changing course is still cheap. The stakes scale from a weekend side project to the largest companies on earth. Amazon's original site tested whether people would buy books over the internet before warehouses and logistics networks existed; the founder famously bought books from distributors as orders arrived. Google, Apple, and virtually every consumer software company now run the same logic continuously under names like experimentation and A/B testing. For an individual with an idea, the MVP mindset is arguably more valuable than any single technique in this guide, because it replaces the question "how do I build my idea?" with the sharper question "what is the cheapest honest test of the belief my idea depends on?" That reframing protects the scarcest resources a founder has, which are not money but time and morale. This guide covers where the concept came from, the reasoning machinery underneath it, the main MVP formats with real historical examples, a concrete working procedure, how to measure and interpret results without fooling yourself, and, importantly, the situations where the whole approach breaks down and something else is called for.

sections.heading: Where the Idea Came From
sections.body: The phrase minimum viable product was coined around 2001 by Frank Robinson, a product-development consultant in Santa Barbara, who used it to describe the smallest product a team could build that would still be worth selling, sized to maximize return on risk for both builder and customer. But the idea's intellectual roots run much deeper. Manufacturing contributed the first strand: the Toyota Production System, developed in postwar Japan by Taiichi Ohno and colleagues, treated overproduction and inventory as waste and prized short feedback cycles in which problems surface immediately. Its Western popularization as lean manufacturing in the 1990s supplied both a vocabulary and a proof that eliminating work which no customer values is a competitive weapon. The second strand came from the scientific method itself: treat every plan as a hypothesis, design the cheapest experiment that could falsify it, and let evidence, not opinion, settle arguments. The third strand was entrepreneurial practice. Steve Blank, a serial Silicon Valley founder turned educator, argued in his 2005 book The Four Steps to the Epiphany that startups are not small versions of large companies; a large company executes a known business model, while a startup is a temporary organization searching for one. His customer development process demanded that founders get out of the building and test their assumptions on real buyers before scaling anything. Eric Ries, who had been Blank's student and cofounded the virtual-world company IMVU, fused these strands into the Lean Startup movement, first on a widely read blog beginning in 2008 and then in the 2011 bestseller The Lean Startup. Ries defined the MVP as the version of a new product which allows a team to collect the maximum amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort, and embedded it in a loop he named build-measure-learn. IMVU supplied the cautionary origin story: the founders spent six months building sophisticated technology on the assumption users would want it as an add-on to existing instant- messaging networks, only to learn from actual users, almost immediately once they finally asked, that the assumption was simply false. The money and code were not the real loss; the six months of foregone learning were. The vocabulary spread with unusual speed through startup accelerators such as Y Combinator, founded in 2005, whose model of small investments and three-month cycles institutionalized rapid tests, and through the 2010s the language of MVPs, pivots, and validated learning became the default dialect of technology entrepreneurship worldwide, taught in business schools and adopted, with varying sincerity, inside corporations and government digital services. Knowing this lineage matters practically: the MVP is not a license to ship shoddy work, which is a corruption of the idea, but the software-age descendant of a century of thought about waste, feedback, and how organizations learn under uncertainty.

sections.heading: Validated Learning and the Build-Measure-Learn Loop
sections.body: The engine underneath every MVP is a feedback loop with three stations. You build the smallest artifact that can test a belief; you measure how real people actually respond to it; you learn, meaning you keep, revise, or abandon the belief based on what the measurement showed. Then the loop runs again with the next belief. Eric Ries called the output of this loop validated learning, and the adjective is the important part. Unvalidated learning is what fills most business plans: conclusions drawn from introspection, from asking friends who want to be encouraging, from surveys where saying yes costs nothing, from the sheer vividness of one's own vision. Validated learning is a conclusion backed by observed behavior of real prospective customers, ideally behavior that cost them something: money, time, reputation, or the effort of switching. The distinction is behavioral economics in miniature. People are poor predictors of their own future behavior and systematically polite to inventors; what they do when a real choice is in front of them is the only evidence with much predictive power. This is why a hundred enthusiastic conversations can be worth less than thirty strangers shown a price and asked to commit. A crucial and widely missed implication is that the loop should be planned backward. Novices plan forward: decide what to build, build it, then look around for numbers to collect. Practitioners plan in reverse: first decide what you need to learn, the specific belief in question; then decide what measurement would genuinely settle it, including the threshold that will count as success, written down before the test; only then design the smallest build that can produce that measurement. Running the loop backward is what keeps the M in MVP honest, because the build is now derived from the test rather than the test rationalized after the build. Speed matters as much as direction. The loop's value compounds with iteration count: a team that completes the circuit every two weeks learns roughly six times as often as a team on a quarterly cycle, and since each pass corrects course, faster loops do not just accumulate learning linearly, they prevent long excursions in wrong directions. This is the honest argument for cutting scope, and it has nothing to do with laziness or low standards; it is the same logic by which a scientist prefers ten quick decisive experiments to one elaborate ambiguous one. Two warnings complete the picture. First, the loop only works if the measure station can fail. A test that cannot come back negative, because success is defined vaguely or the metric always drifts upward, is theater, and theater is more dangerous than ignorance because it feels like knowledge. Second, learning must actually change behavior; a team that measures, learns the idea is weak, and proceeds anyway because sunk costs and enthusiasm carry the day has paid learning's price and thrown away the goods. The rest of this guide is essentially detailed technique for making each of these three stations, build, measure, learn, hard to fool.

sections.heading: What Minimum and Viable Actually Mean
sections.body: The two adjectives in minimum viable product pull against each other, and finding the point of balance is the core judgment call of the whole method. Cut too little and you waste months building features the test never needed; cut too much and the artifact is so weak that customers reject it for reasons that have nothing to do with your idea, giving you a false negative. A useful way to locate the balance is to ask: what is the smallest thing such that, if customers reject it, I will genuinely believe the idea is in trouble, rather than blaming the execution? Henrik Kniberg, a coach at Spotify, drew the most famous illustration of the principle. Building a car by delivering one wheel, then a chassis, then a body is minimal but never viable; the customer can do nothing with a wheel. Delivering a skateboard, then a scooter, then a bicycle, then a motorbike, then a car is viable at every step: each stage is a complete, usable answer to the underlying need, which is getting from place to place, and each stage teaches you something about riders. The lesson is that you slice through the problem vertically, delivering a thin but complete path from need to satisfaction, rather than horizontally, delivering polished components of an unusable whole. Viability also has a quality floor, and it is higher than beginners assume in one specific place: the core action. Users forgive a plain design, missing settings, and manual workarounds behind the scenes, but if the one thing the product promises is unreliable, slow, or confusing, the test measures your bugs rather than their demand. The practical rule is severe narrowness with adequate depth: one user type, one problem, one path through the product, working well; everything else absent, faked, or done by hand. Minimum, meanwhile, is relative to risk, not a fixed size. If the risky assumption is that people want the outcome at all, the minimum artifact might be a one-page description and a sign-up button, buildable in a day. If desirability is already proven and the risk is that your approach can deliver the outcome, the minimum artifact may be a genuine working core that takes months; SpaceX could not test reusable rockets with a landing page. A related distinction worth keeping: an MVP is not a prototype and not a beta. A prototype answers an internal question, can this be built and how, and is typically shown to insiders. A beta is a nearly finished product being hardened. The MVP sits between, an externally facing experiment about the market. Finally, minimum is bounded by ethics and law: a payments MVP must actually safeguard money, a health MVP must not dispense dangerous advice, and faking those is not lean, it is negligent. Within those floors, the discipline is always the same question asked repeatedly: what can we remove and still get a verdict we would trust?

sections.heading: Leap-of-Faith Assumptions: Finding the Belief to Test
sections.body: Every venture idea, stated plainly, is a bundle of assumptions, and the first analytical act of MVP work is to unbundle it and rank the pieces by how likely they are to be wrong and how fatal it is if they are. Ries called the load-bearing ones leap-of-faith assumptions, the beliefs the whole enterprise stands on. They cluster into four recurring families, and naming them helps you search systematically. Desirability assumptions concern the customer: a specific group of people has this problem, feels it acutely enough to act, and would prefer your kind of solution to what they do today, including the ever-present competitor of doing nothing. Viability assumptions concern money: those people, or someone on their behalf, will pay enough, and can be reached and converted at a cost that leaves a margin; the entire economics of many consumer businesses collapses on the quiet assumption that customers can be acquired for less than they are worth. Feasibility assumptions concern delivery: your team can actually build and operate the thing at the promised quality and cost, at scale. Growth assumptions concern spread: usage begets more usage through word of mouth, virality, sales repeatability, or retention strong enough to compound. To work with these, write each one as a falsifiable hypothesis with a number in it, in the form: we believe that a specific group will take a specific observable action at at least a specific rate, and we will know within a specific time. Compare the vague "restaurants want better scheduling software" with the testable "at least 4 of the 20 independent restaurant managers we approach this month will prepay 50 dollars for early access to a scheduling tool." The vague form can never lose an argument; the sharp form can lose, which is exactly what makes it capable of teaching. Then rank. Two axes suffice: how uncertain are we, and how catastrophic is being wrong. The assumption that scores high on both is the riskiest assumption, and it, not the most interesting or most technical assumption, is what the first MVP must test. Teams of engineers reliably get this backward, gravitating to feasibility because building is the fun part and because it is the risk they know how to retire; yet in most software ventures feasibility is the least doubtful family, while desirability, the unglamorous question of whether anyone cares, is where ventures actually die. A written map of assumptions has a second benefit beyond choosing tests: it converts founder disagreements from clashes of conviction into differences about which experiment to run first, which is a far cheaper kind of argument. Revisit the map after every test, because retired risks change the ranking, and yesterday's second-riskiest assumption is promoted to today's target.

sections.heading: Smoke Tests: Landing Pages, Preorders, and Ads
sections.body: The cheapest family of MVPs sells the product before it exists and measures who reaches for their wallet. The classic form is the landing page test, sometimes called a smoke test: a single web page that states the value proposition as if the product were real, with a price if pricing is part of the question, and one call to action, join the waiting list, request access, or preorder. Traffic is then driven to the page, most commonly with small paid search or social media ad campaigns costing tens to a few hundred dollars, targeted at the customer segment in question. The measurements are the click-through rate on the ads, which tests whether the promise stops the right people mid-scroll, and the conversion rate on the page, which tests whether the fuller pitch persuades them to act. As rough calibration, cold-traffic landing page conversion to an email signup commonly falls between 5 and 15 percent for a resonant offer, and paid-search click-through above roughly 2 percent suggests the phrasing of the promise has found a nerve; numbers far below these bands, after honest attempts at fixing copy and targeting, are evidence about demand itself. The strength of commitment can be escalated deliberately: an email address is weak evidence, a scheduled call is stronger, a refundable deposit stronger still, and a paid preorder is close to definitive. Each escalation filters out politeness. The approach has famous successes. In 2007 Drew Houston, unable to demonstrate file-synchronization software whose hard parts were still unbuilt, posted a three-minute screen-capture video of Dropbox working, seeded with in-jokes for the technical early adopters he needed; the beta waiting list reportedly grew from around 5,000 to some 75,000 people almost overnight, validating demand before the product could be widely distributed. Tim Ferriss has described testing book titles with competing ad campaigns before publication. Crowdfunding platforms such as Kickstarter, launched in 2009, institutionalized the preorder smoke test for physical goods: the Pebble smartwatch raised over 10 million dollars in 2012 from more than 68,000 backers, proof of demand that no survey could have supplied. Ethics and law require care here. Collecting emails for a possible future product is uncontroversial; taking money requires either genuine intent and ability to deliver within the stated expectations or immediate refunds, and advertising a product that does not exist, without disclosure that it is upcoming, can cross into deceptive-practice territory in many jurisdictions. The honest formulation is transparency about status, coming soon, join the waitlist, reserve your spot, which loses little signal. The limits of smoke tests are equally important to internalize: they measure attraction, not satisfaction or retention. A strong signup rate proves the promise resonates; it says nothing about whether the delivered product will keep its users, which is a different assumption requiring a different test, and many teams have scaled on smoke-test enthusiasm straight into a retention cliff.

sections.heading: Concierge MVPs: Doing It by Hand
sections.body: A concierge MVP delivers the product's outcome entirely through manual human effort, openly, with no software pretending otherwise. The name comes from the hotel concierge, and the canonical story is Food on the Table, an Austin startup founded in 2010 whose eventual product generated weekly meal plans and grocery lists matched to local supermarket sales. Its founder, Manuel Rosso, began with exactly one customer. Each week he personally reviewed one family's preferences, checked the sale flyers, composed a meal plan by hand, and delivered it for a few dollars, then repeated the process as he slowly added families. Nothing about this scaled, and that was the point: before writing recommendation software, he learned precisely what customers valued, week after week, from paying users, and only automated steps when the manual load forced it. The company was acquired by the Food Network in 2014. The concierge pattern shines when the risky assumption is about the shape of the value itself: what exactly should the service do, for whom, with what variations. Because a human is executing every step, you observe the messy reality of the work, discover which parts customers actually care about, and can change the offering overnight without a development cycle. It also produces revenue evidence early, since people are paying for outcomes, not for software. Its costs are equally clear: it consumes founder time voraciously, serves only a handful of customers, and tests nothing about whether the eventual automated product will be usable or whether the economics survive when a server replaces a human being paid nothing. The pattern therefore fits early, narrow, high-touch learning, and it must eventually hand off to automation guided by what was learned. Aardvark, a question-answering service later acquired by Google for a reported 50 million dollars, ran a related play: for a period, humans behind the curtain routed questions to appropriate answerers while the founders studied what routing algorithm would be worth building. Zappos, the online shoe retailer eventually bought by Amazon in a deal valued around 1.2 billion dollars, began in 1999 with founder Nick Swinmurn photographing shoes in local stores and buying pairs at retail only after a customer ordered online, personally handling fulfillment; the test cost almost nothing and established that people would buy shoes without trying them on, then the hard logistics were built on validated demand. When running a concierge test yourself, three disciplines keep it honest. Charge something, because free concierge service measures your likability, not demand. Write down each week what you did manually and which steps customers noticed or praised, because that log is the specification of the future product. And predefine the graduation trigger, the throughput or waitlist size at which you will stop hand-serving and start automating, so the comfortable ritual of personal service does not quietly become the business.

sections.heading: Wizard of Oz and Piecemeal MVPs
sections.body: A Wizard of Oz MVP presents customers with what appears to be a finished, automated product, while behind the interface humans secretly perform the work. The name refers to the man behind the curtain in the 1939 film, and the technique inherits a lineage from human-computer interaction research, where experimenters simulated speech recognizers and dialogue systems with hidden operators as far back as the 1970s and 1980s to study how people would talk to machines that did not yet exist. In business use, the customer experience is real, the pricing is real, the delivered outcome is real; only the mechanism is simulated. This differs from the concierge pattern in exactly one dimension, disclosure: the concierge is openly human, the wizard hides it. That hidden-ness is what makes the pattern powerful for testing interaction assumptions, because customers behave as they would toward the real product, with no politeness discount and no coaching. It tests the interface, the workflow, the pricing, and the demand simultaneously, at the cost of terrible unit economics that you accept temporarily because learning, not margin, is the product. The pattern has quiet but wide use: early automated-sounding services for scheduling, transcription, personal shopping, and document review have commonly launched with humans doing most of the work while volume was low, using the interim period both to learn and to accumulate the labeled examples that later trained the automation. The approach carries two specific obligations. First, privacy: if users believe a machine is reading their messages or documents, but humans are, you are courting both betrayal and legal exposure; terms of service must genuinely cover human processing, and sensitive categories of data raise the bar further. Second, an exit plan: the economics only make sense if the manual period is bounded and instrumented, so measure minutes of human labor per transaction from day one and watch whether the trend line, as you gradually automate steps, plausibly reaches a viable cost. A cousin of these patterns is the piecemeal MVP, which assembles the experience from existing off-the- shelf tools rather than hidden labor: a business run from a form builder, a spreadsheet, a payment link, and a group chat can simulate a surprising fraction of software ideas with no code at all. Groupon began in 2008 as a WordPress blog where deals were posted manually and coupons were generated as PDFs emailed to buyers; the founders proved that group buying moved real money before building a platform, and within two years the company was one of the fastest-growing in history. The modern no-code ecosystem, form tools, workflow automators, website builders, database front-ends, has made piecemeal MVPs dramatically cheaper since the late 2010s, and for most non-technical founders it is now the default first move: if your idea can be faked convincingly with rented parts and some evening labor, it almost never deserves custom code yet.

sections.heading: The Single-Feature Product
sections.body: When the earlier, cheaper test formats have done their work, or when the risky assumption genuinely requires software in users' hands, the appropriate MVP is often a single-feature product: a real, working piece of software that does exactly one thing for one kind of user, with everything else deferred. The discipline is in the phrase exactly one thing. The founding versions of several famous products were radically narrower than their later selves, and studying them is instructive. Instagram began life in 2010 as Burbn, a cluttered location check-in app with plans, points, and photos; usage data showed people ignored everything but the photo sharing, so founders Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger deleted the rest and shipped an app that did three tightly linked things, square photos, filters, and a feed, famously gaining 25,000 users on its first day and a million within about three months. Twitter emerged in 2006 from a podcasting company, Odeo, as an internal side project for posting 140-character status messages, and for years resisted feature growth that would blur that single verb. The first iPhone shipped without an app store, copy and paste, or multitasking; Apple bet the launch on a few core experiences done exceptionally well. The engineering implication of a single-feature MVP is a deliberately modest quality bar everywhere except the core loop. Authentication can be borrowed from existing identity providers, payments from a hosted checkout, hosting from a platform service; the interface can be plain; the admin tools can be a database console used by hand. But the core action, the one the product exists for, must be genuinely good, because that is the variable under test. Speed of iteration after launch matters more than polish at launch: instrument the product from the first day so you can see where users arrive from, where they stall, and whether they return, since a single-feature MVP is less a launch than the opening move of a measurement campaign. Choose scope with a timebox rather than a feature list: decide, for instance, that the first version gets six weeks of evenings or one month of full-time work, and let that budget force the cuts, because effort estimates for software are systematically optimistic and an open-ended scope will silently grow. A useful planning trick is the demo script: write, before building, the two-minute walkthrough you want to be able to perform for a stranger, then build only what that script touches. Everything not in the script is, by construction, not minimum. The single-feature MVP's characteristic failure mode is the quiet accumulation of just-one-more features before anyone outside the team has used it; the countermeasure is a standing rule that no second feature is started until the first has been used by strangers and the numbers have been read. Narrowness is not a compromise here; it is the instrument's precision.

sections.heading: Running the Test: A Working Procedure
sections.body: What follows is a concrete, general-purpose procedure for taking an idea to a first verdict in roughly four to eight weeks of part-time effort, suitable for a software or service idea; adjust proportions to your domain. It compresses the reasoning machinery covered throughout this guide, hypothesis framing, test selection, honest measurement, into an executable sequence. Treat the thresholds you set in the early steps as promises to your future self: they are cheap to write down now and nearly impossible to set honestly after data arrives, because motivated reasoning will bend any ambiguous number toward continuing. Note also what the procedure does not include: branding, incorporation, pitch decks, and logo design, all of which are pleasant, none of which produce learning, and all of which can wait until something real has been validated. The procedure assumes you can reach at least a few dozen members of your target segment; if you cannot reach customers at all, that inability is itself the riskiest assumption and must be attacked first, because a product no one can be told about cannot be tested or sold. Expect the full sequence to cost between a few hundred and a couple of thousand dollars, mostly advertising spend and tool subscriptions, and expect to run it more than once: a single pass rarely settles more than one assumption, and the second pass is nearly always sharper, because the first taught you the segment's vocabulary, objections, and gathering places.
steps: Write the idea as one sentence naming the customer, the problem, and the change you promise: for busy parents, weeknight dinner planning, cut to ten minutes a week.
List every assumption the idea depends on across desirability, viability, feasibility, and growth; aim for at least fifteen written statements.
Score each assumption 1-5 for uncertainty and for how fatal being wrong would be; multiply, rank, and circle the top score as the riskiest assumption.
Rewrite the riskiest assumption as a falsifiable hypothesis with numbers and a deadline: at least 10 of 100 targeted visitors will leave an email address within two weeks.
Choose the cheapest test format that could genuinely settle it: interviews plus a landing page for desirability, a priced preorder for viability, a concierge week for value shape.
Build the artifact in a strict timebox of days, not weeks, using rented parts wherever possible; write the two-minute demo script first and build only what it touches.
Recruit real strangers from the target segment through ads, communities, or direct outreach; exclude friends and family from the data even if you let them look.
Run the test until you hit the predeclared sample size or deadline, resisting every mid-test urge to redefine success; log every observation, including the embarrassing ones.
Compare results to the threshold you wrote in step 4 and write a one-page verdict: validated, refuted, or ambiguous, plus the single biggest surprise.
Decide explicitly among persevere, pivot, or stop; then promote the next-riskiest assumption and run the loop again, carrying forward what the last test taught.

sections.heading: Measuring Without Fooling Yourself
sections.body: The measurement station of the loop is where most self-deception lives, and the antidote is a small amount of metric literacy. Ries drew the field's central distinction: vanity metrics versus actionable metrics. Vanity metrics are numbers that can only go up and flatter every decision equally: cumulative sign-ups, total downloads, page views, press mentions, social media followers. They rise whether or not the product is working, because they never subtract the people who left. Actionable metrics tie a specific number to a specific decision and can go down: the percentage of new users who complete the core action in their first session, the percentage still active four weeks later, the conversion from trial to paid, revenue per customer against cost to acquire that customer. The single most diagnostic instrument for an MVP is cohort analysis. Instead of one blended activity curve, group users by the week they arrived and track each group separately over time: of the people who started in week one, what fraction returned in their second week, their fourth, their eighth? Every cohort traces a retention curve, and the shape is the verdict. A curve that falls and then flattens at some meaningful level means a core of people has real use for the thing; a curve that decays smoothly toward zero means you are refilling a leaking bucket, and acquisition spend is disguising product failure. Watching whether successive cohorts flatten higher, as you improve the product, is the cleanest read of progress an early team can have. A popular organizing scheme is the pirate-metrics funnel, AARRR, named by investor Dave McClure in 2007 for its initials: acquisition, do the right people arrive; activation, do they experience the core value once; retention, do they come back; revenue, does money change hands; referral, do they bring others. An MVP rarely needs all five instrumented; it needs the one or two stages the current hypothesis lives in, measured carefully. Numbers alone, though, under-determine causes, which is why quantitative data should be paired with qualitative observation: watch five users attempt the product while thinking aloud, in person or by screen share, and you will usually learn why the funnel leaks where it does; usability research going back to Jakob Nielsen's work in the 1990s suggests a handful of observed sessions surfaces the large majority of blocking problems. Guard finally against the statistics of small samples. With thirty users, a difference between 20 percent and 30 percent conversion is comfortably within the range chance produces; resist celebrating or despairing over movements that a coin-flip model explains, and when a comparison truly matters, run it as a controlled A/B test with a predeclared sample size. The discipline in one sentence: decide in advance which number would change your mind, measure that number cleanly, and let it.

sections.heading: Talking to Customers: Interviews That Yield Truth
sections.body: Interviews are the cheapest test instrument available, usable before anything is built at all, but they produce truth only when conducted against the grain of ordinary politeness. The failure mode is universal: you describe your idea with visible enthusiasm, the other person likes you, and they say it sounds great, which costs them nothing and teaches you nothing. Rob Fitzpatrick's short 2013 book The Mom Test named the corrective principle: design questions so honest answers are possible even from your own mother, which means questions about the customer's life, not your idea. Three rules carry most of the weight. Talk about their past, not their future: "how do you handle scheduling today, and what did you do last week?" instead of "would you use an app that did this?", because recalled behavior is evidence while predicted behavior is mostly courtesy. Ask about specifics and costs: what happens when it goes wrong, how long does it take, what does it cost, what have they already tried and abandoned; a person who has never attempted to solve a problem, with money, time, or even a spreadsheet, is telling you the problem is not painful enough, whatever they say about it. And withhold your idea until the end, if you present it at all, so the conversation cannot collapse into a pitch. Structure a session in three movements over twenty to thirty minutes: open with their context and role; go deep on the last few occurrences of the problem, walking through one episode step by step; close by testing commitment, and here the currency matters more than the words. Advice is cheap; introductions, scheduled follow-ups, requests to be a pilot user, and above all money are expensive, and only expensive signals count. A useful ladder of commitment runs: kind words, time, reputation, money; try always to end an enthusiastic interview by asking for the next rung, and treat refusal as data, not rudeness. Practicalities: recruit interviewees from the actual segment, through communities, cold outreach, or intercepts where they gather, and expect to need roughly fifteen to thirty conversations before patterns stabilize; take verbatim notes or record with permission, because memory edits interviews into agreement with hopes; and separate the roles of asking and interpreting when you can, since the interviewer's investment biases live coding of answers. Know also what interviews cannot do. They map problems, vocabularies, current workarounds, and willingness signals, and they are unmatched for discovering which problem to solve; they are weak at predicting adoption of genuinely novel behaviors, where even honest people cannot forecast themselves, which is why interview findings should feed, not replace, behavioral tests like the smoke tests and working MVPs described elsewhere in this guide. Interviews find the target; behavior confirms the hit.

sections.heading: Reading the Verdict: Pivot, Persevere, or Stop
sections.body: Sooner or later the loop delivers a verdict, and the learn station becomes a decision: persevere on the current course, pivot to a revised strategy, or stop entirely. A pivot, in Ries's precise usage, is not any change and certainly not mere failure; it is a structured course correction that changes one core element of the strategy while keeping the learning and usually much of the machinery. The recognized varieties are worth knowing because they expand the option space beyond the false binary of push on or give up. A zoom-in pivot makes one feature the whole product, as when Burbn became Instagram by deleting everything but photos. A customer-segment pivot keeps the product but aims it at the people who turned out to love it, rather than the people the plan predicted; the enterprise chat product that becomes a small-team tool, or vice versa. A problem pivot keeps the customer but attacks a different pain discovered during research. A platform pivot turns an application into infrastructure others build on, as Slack grew from the internal chat tool of a failed game company, Glitch, whose studio Tiny Speck pivoted in 2013, or as Shopify emerged from a snowboard shop whose founders realized the store software was the business. A business-model or channel pivot changes how money or distribution works, high-touch sales versus self-serve, ads versus subscriptions. YouTube began in 2005 as a video-dating site and pivoted within months when uploads were general videos, not dating profiles; Twitter rose from Odeo's pivot away from podcasting. The hard part is not the taxonomy but the trigger, because evidence is usually mixed and hope is inventive. Three signals argue for pivoting: the predeclared threshold was missed and post-hoc explanations are doing heavy lifting; growth continues only when paid for, with cohort retention curves decaying toward zero; and the qualitative channel keeps surfacing the same alternative use, segment, or problem, an energy gradient pointing somewhere specific. Three signals argue for persevering: a subset of users retains strongly even if small; the misses trace to executable flaws, onboarding, messaging, a broken step, rather than indifference to the outcome; and each loop's changes move the focal metric. Stopping, the least discussed option, is rational when repeated pivots have exhausted the plausible strategy space, when no identifiable subgroup retains, or when the opportunity cost of the team's years now exceeds the venture's honest expected value; a clean stop preserves capital, reputation, and the energy to run the next loop on a better idea. Whatever the call, schedule it: regular pivot-or-persevere meetings, every four to eight weeks, with the metrics reviewed against the written thresholds, convert an emotional cliff into a routine governance act, which is precisely what makes honest answers survivable.

sections.heading: Testing Price and Willingness to Pay
sections.body: Pricing is the assumption teams defer longest and should test earliest, because a product people admire but will not pay for is a hobby, and because price is itself information that changes every other measurement: free users and paying users are different populations with different behavior, and only the second population proves a business. The core principle is that willingness to pay is measured by behavior in the presence of a price, not by asking. Survey questions of the form "would you pay 20 dollars a month?" reliably overstate demand several-fold, since agreeing costs nothing and refusing feels rude. Behavioral tests come in escalating strength. Weakest but still useful is the priced landing page: state a price and measure whether conversion collapses relative to an unpriced version; Buffer's founder famously inserted a pricing-plans page between the landing page and the signup form and watched which plans drew clicks before writing the software. Stronger is the pre-sale: collect actual payment, refundable, for delivery at a stated later date, the mechanism crowdfunding industrialized. Strongest is simply selling: in business-to-business markets, founders can and should attempt to close paid pilot agreements, even letters of intent with numbers on them, before the product exists in full; a sales conversation that ends in a signed pilot at 500 dollars a month has tested desirability, price point, and the sales channel in one motion. When you need to estimate an acceptable range before testing, two survey instruments are better than naive asking because they triangulate. The Van Westendorp price-sensitivity meter, published in 1976, asks four questions, at what price would this be so cheap you doubt its quality, a bargain, getting expensive, and too expensive to consider, and the crossing points of the cumulative curves bracket an acceptable band. Conjoint analysis, older still in market research, forces respondents to trade features against price across repeated choices, extracting implied values from the pattern of picks rather than from stated numbers. Treat both as instruments for locating the first test price, not as verdicts. Structural choices matter as much as level: one-time purchase versus subscription, per-seat versus flat, freemium versus free trial versus paid-only. Freemium in particular is dangerous for MVPs, because free tiers flood your metrics with users who were never candidates to pay, obscuring exactly the signal you need; a paid-only or trial-then-paid MVP yields cleaner learning even if it grows slower. Two practical notes close the topic. First, founders systematically underprice, both from fear and from comparing to consumer software; in business markets especially, low prices can suppress demand by signaling unseriousness, and raising price is among the most common successful early pivots. Second, price tests must be honest: charging real money creates real obligations of delivery or refund, and discovered prices should be honored for the customers who revealed them.

sections.heading: Where MVP Thinking Breaks Down
sections.body: The MVP is a tool with a domain of validity, and intellectual honesty requires drawing its boundaries. The method assumes iteration is cheap, failure is survivable, and early customers tolerate roughness; where those assumptions fail, the method must be modified or set aside. Safety-critical and regulated domains are the clearest case. Medical devices, drugs, aviation software, and financial custody cannot ethically or legally be probed on the public with rough drafts; regulators such as the FDA exist precisely to forbid it, and clinical trials are society's own, highly formalized validation loop. Lean techniques still apply upstream, interviews with clinicians, paper prototypes, simulated workflows, but the shippable-experiment core does not transfer. Hardware and deep technology stretch the method differently: iteration cycles are long and capital-intensive, so teams shift learning onto cheaper proxies, renders and preorder campaigns for demand, engineering prototypes for feasibility, and accept that some bets, a rocket, a fusion reactor, a new battery chemistry, resolve only after years of committed spending; for such ventures the honest tool is milestone-based risk retirement rather than weekly loops. Network-effect products face the cold-start problem: a marketplace or social product with no participants delivers no value at any size of feature set, so the minimum in MVP must include a seeding strategy, which is why successful examples begin in one niche, one campus, one city, Facebook at Harvard in 2004, Airbnb in San Francisco during conferences, and only then expand. Brand- sensitive contexts, established companies, and winner-take-most markets raise the reputational cost of public roughness; the standard mitigations are testing under a separate brand name, in a limited geography, or with a private cohort, so the experiment's blast radius is contained. There are also intrinsic criticisms to take seriously. A stream of incremental MVP tests optimizes locally and can never surface ideas customers cannot articulate; the two standard, only partly satisfying, responses are that vision chooses the hill and experiments choose the path up it, and that some category-creating products, the iPhone among them, were built on conviction plus taste with validation arriving only at launch. Competitors can observe a public test and move; secrecy has costs too, and most teams overrate this risk, but it is not zero. And the method's vocabulary is corruptible: "MVP" used as an excuse to ship a broken product to paying customers is not lean, it is a quality failure wearing lean's clothes, and it burns exactly the early adopters whose goodwill the method depends on. When a test fails in ways that feel wrong, check the meta-assumptions: was the sample from the true segment, was the artifact viable enough to be a fair test, was the threshold realistic? A refuted hypothesis is learning; a badly run test is merely noise, and telling the two apart is the last skill this method demands.

sections.heading: After Validation: From MVP to Product
sections.body: A validated MVP is a beginning, not an arrival, and the transition it triggers is where many teams stumble a second time. What validation actually confers is narrow: evidence that a specific group takes a specific valuable action at a rate that clears your threshold. The work that follows divides into three tracks that compete for the same scarce hours, and the failure pattern is starving whichever track the founders enjoy least. The first track is deepening value for the users you have: closing the gap between the MVP's rough edges and a product whose core loop is reliable, fast, and self-explanatory, because the retention curves that validated you will sag as you move beyond forgiving early adopters, the enthusiasts Geoffrey Moore's 1991 book Crossing the Chasm distinguishes sharply from the pragmatic early majority, who demand whole, dependable products. The second track is paying down deliberate debt. An MVP is built on shortcuts, manual steps, rented parts, code written for speed, and each shortcut was a loan taken against the future; now inventory them, because scale calls those loans. Concierge and Wizard of Oz mechanics must be automated in the order the labor log dictates; the analytics duct tape must become instrumentation you trust; security and reliability move from best-effort to obligation the moment strangers depend on you, and in many jurisdictions data-protection law, such as Europe's GDPR in force since 2018, applies to you at any size. The third track is building the growth machine: converting whatever acquisition channel the test used, often unscalable founder hustle, into repeatable economics, measured by the ratio of a customer's lifetime value to acquisition cost, with a common rule of thumb demanding roughly three to one before spending aggressively, and by Sean Ellis's much-used product-market-fit survey question, what percentage of users would be very disappointed if the product disappeared, where above roughly 40 percent has been treated as a green light since he proposed it around 2009. Do not, however, discard the experimental engine that got you here. The mature form of MVP practice inside a growing product is continuous experimentation, feature flags, A/B tests, staged rollouts, the machinery with which large technology companies run thousands of concurrent tests, and the leap-of-faith map should simply refill with the next tier of assumptions: new segments, new geographies, pricing changes, adjacent problems. Paul Graham's dictum from Y Combinator, do things that don't scale, has a second clause too rarely quoted: the unscalable things are how you learn what the scalable version must preserve. Teams that treat validation as permission to stop listening rebuild, at larger cost, the ignorance the MVP existed to cure. The loop never ends; it just runs on a bigger machine, with more at stake, and with a team that now knows, from evidence rather than hope, why its customers come.

guides.title: Testing Demand Before You Build
guides.summary: How to find out whether anyone will actually buy a product before spending months building it: evidence hierarchies, customer interviews, smoke tests, preorders, pricing experiments, and how to read the results without fooling yourself.

sections.heading: Why Products Fail: The Case for Testing Demand
sections.body: Most new products do not fail because they are badly engineered, badly designed or badly marketed. They fail because nobody wanted them enough to pay for them, and the people who built them found this out last, after the money was spent. When the research firm CB Insights analyzed post-mortems written by founders of failed startups, the single most cited cause — named in roughly 35 to 42 percent of cases across several editions of the study — was "no market need." The graveyard is well stocked with expensively engineered answers to questions nobody was asking. Webvan raised over 800 million dollars in the late 1990s to build automated grocery warehouses before discovering that not enough 1999-era customers would change their shopping habits to fill them; it burned through the money and collapsed in 2001. Juicero raised about 120 million dollars for a beautifully machined 700-dollar machine that squeezed proprietary juice packets, and folded within months of a journalist demonstrating that human hands squeezed the packets just as well. The Segway was engineering triumph and demand fiasco in one chassis: its inventor predicted it would reach a million units faster than any product in history, and it sold roughly 140,000 in nearly two decades. In each case the fatal question — will enough people pay enough money for this? — was answerable early and cheaply, and was instead answered late and catastrophically. Testing demand before you build is the discipline of reversing that order. The logic rests on a simple asymmetry. Building a product costs months or years and, for physical goods or serious software, sums that are hard to recover; running a demand test costs days or weeks and amounts of money that a mistake can afford. If a hundred-dollar experiment has even a modest chance of preventing a hundred-thousand-dollar error, its expected value is enormous. The approach has an intellectual lineage. Eric Ries's 2011 book The Lean Startup popularized the vocabulary — minimum viable product, validated learning, build-measure-learn — drawing on Steve Blank's earlier customer development method, which insisted that "no business plan survives first contact with customers" and that a startup's real job is not executing a plan but searching for one that works. Behind both stands the ordinary logic of science: treat your business idea as a hypothesis, not a fact, and design the cheapest possible experiment that could prove it wrong. None of this guarantees success. Demand tests produce noisy, sometimes misleading signals, and a few celebrated products would likely have tested poorly before they existed. But the base rates are brutal — most new consumer packaged goods fail, most apps are abandoned within days of download, most startups die — and in a game with brutal base rates, cheap information is the closest thing to an unfair advantage that a founder, a product manager or a small-business owner can buy.

sections.heading: The Hierarchy of Evidence
sections.body: Not all evidence of demand is worth the same, and the single most useful mental tool in this entire subject is a ranking of evidence by how much it costs the customer to produce it. At the bottom sits the cheapest signal of all: opinion. "That's a great idea, I'd definitely buy that" costs the speaker nothing and is contaminated by politeness, by optimism about a hypothetical future self, and by the social awkwardness of discouraging an enthusiastic founder to their face. Survey responses live here too: decades of consumer research show that stated purchase intent overpredicts actual purchase, often by a factor of two or more, and the gap widens for novel products the respondent has never seen in the wild. One rung up sits verified interest: the customer spends a little attention — clicking an advertisement, reading a page, watching a demo video to the end. Above that sits identity: the customer hands over something slightly costly and personal, most commonly an email address, sometimes a phone number, which converts a stranger into a countable, re-contactable lead. Higher still sits time: the customer sits for a thirty-minute interview about their current workflow, attends a demo, or completes an onboarding questionnaire for a product that does not yet exist. Above time sits public commitment: a signed letter of intent from a business, a preorder pledge on a crowdfunding page, a place on a waiting list taken under their real name. And at the very top sits the only evidence that fully survives contact with reality: money. A paid deposit, a completed preorder, a signed purchase order, a first month's subscription fee — each is a costly, falsifiable act that the customer had every opportunity not to perform. The practical rule that follows: whenever possible, buy your information from higher on the ladder. A hundred enthusiastic survey responses are worth less than ten strangers who clicked a paid advertisement, which are worth less than three who entered a credit card, which are worth less than one who paid a nonrefundable deposit. The ladder also explains the design of every technique in this field. Interviews are structured to extract facts about past behavior rather than opinions about the future, because past behavior is something the customer has already paid for. Landing pages exist to convert vague interest into countable emails. Preorder buttons exist to convert emails into money. A second, subtler principle rides along: the evidence must come from strangers. Friends, family and colleagues produce systematically inflated signals because their incentive is to support you, not to be right. The entire apparatus of demand testing can be summarized as machinery for obtaining, from strangers, at the lowest possible cost to you, signals that cost them as much as possible to fake.

sections.heading: Customer Discovery Interviews That Don't Lie
sections.body: The cheapest demand instrument is a conversation, and it is also the easiest to ruin. The failure mode is so common it has a name: asking people whether they like your idea. Almost everyone, almost always, will say yes — your mother most of all, which is why Rob Fitzpatrick's 2013 handbook on the craft is titled The Mom Test. Its central rule: a good customer interview never mentions your idea at all. Instead it interrogates the customer's life as it already is, because the past is factual and the future is performance. Three principles carry most of the weight. First, talk about their life, not your idea — you are hunting for problems they demonstrably have, not reactions to a solution you are proud of. Second, ask about specifics in the past, not generics or hypotheticals in the future. "Would you use a tool that did X?" invites theater. "Walk me through the last time you dealt with X — what did you do, what did it cost, what did you try?" invites facts. Third, listen for what they have already done about the problem, because effort and money already spent are the only reliable measures of how much a problem hurts. A customer who describes cobbling together a spreadsheet, hiring a part-time assistant, or paying for a half-working competitor is showing you a wound; a customer who says a problem is "annoying" but has never lifted a finger about it is showing you a shrug. Concrete questions that earn their keep: When did this last happen? How often? What does it cost you when it does — in hours, in money, in trouble with whom? What have you tried? What did you pay for that? Why did you stop using it? Who else suffers from this? What happens if you just do nothing? Danger signs in the answers include compliments ("that's so cool"), generalities ("I usually," "I always," "I would definitely"), and futures ("I'd pay for that" — a phrase that costs nothing and is worth the same). When you hear fluff, deflect the compliment and dig for a specific past incident. Mechanics matter less than discipline, but a few norms help: interview one person at a time, not groups, since groups converge on polite consensus; take verbatim notes or record with permission, because memory launders answers into what you hoped to hear; aim for something like ten to twenty interviews within a narrowly defined customer segment, and expect the strong patterns to surface within the first dozen if the segment is truly narrow; keep recruiting until you can predict a new interviewee's answers before they speak, which is the practical signal of saturation. Interviews cannot prove people will buy — that evidence lives higher on the ladder — but they are unmatched for discovering which problem is worth testing, what words customers use to describe it, and what they already pay, all of which every later experiment will be built from.

sections.heading: Framing a Falsifiable Hypothesis
sections.body: An experiment without a hypothesis is a mood board. Before running any demand test, write down — actually write down, before collecting a single data point — three things: the claim being tested, the evidence that would support it, and the threshold below which you will treat the claim as unsupported. A usable demand hypothesis names a specific customer, a specific problem, a specific alternative they use today, and a specific exchange of value. Compare "people would love an easier way to manage receipts," which can never be wrong, with "freelance designers in the United States who file quarterly taxes will pay 12 dollars a month for automatic receipt capture, because they currently lose two or more hours a month to manual sorting." The second version can fail, which is precisely what makes it worth testing. Each clause is load-bearing: the customer clause tells you who to recruit and where to advertise; the problem and alternative clauses come from interviews and tell you what the landing page must say; the price clause turns the test into a purchase decision rather than an applause meter. Next, identify the riskiest assumption — the one belief that, if false, kills the business regardless of everything else — and aim the first test squarely at it. Founders habitually test the assumption they find most interesting (usually "can we build it?") instead of the one most likely to be fatal (usually "will anyone pay?"). Technical risk is real for rockets and rare for software; for most products the fatal assumption is demand, and it should be tested first because it is also usually the cheapest to test. Then fix your success threshold in advance. The number itself matters less than when you choose it: a threshold chosen after the data arrives will always, mysteriously, sit just below whatever the data shows. Thresholds can be borrowed from public benchmarks — for cold traffic arriving on a well-made landing page, email signup rates in the low tens of percent are common and healthy, while purchase or deposit conversion in the low single digits of percent is more typical — but the better anchor is your own business arithmetic: work backward from the customer-acquisition cost your intended price can support, and ask what conversion rate at the test's traffic cost would make the arithmetic close. Finally, decide the decision rule: above threshold, proceed to the next, more expensive test; near threshold, revise the offer or audience and rerun; below threshold, change something fundamental or stop. Writing the rule down beforehand is a commitment device against the most predictable failure in all of this, which is not bad data but motivated interpretation of ambiguous data. A hypothesis document need not be long — half a page suffices — but teams that skip it almost invariably emerge from their experiments having "learned a lot" and decided nothing, which is the most expensive possible outcome: the cost of the test without the benefit of the verdict.

sections.heading: Smoke Tests and Landing Pages
sections.body: The workhorse of demand testing is the smoke test: present the product as if it existed, invite a real action, and count who acts. Its standard form is a landing page — a single web page describing the product's promise, with one call to action — plus a source of strangers to show it to. The name descends from an older hardware tradition of powering a circuit to see whether it smokes, and the spirit is the same: apply real current, watch for the telltale sign. A landing page test has four working parts. The promise: a headline stating, in the customer's own vocabulary (harvested from interviews), what problem is solved and for whom — not a list of features but an outcome, with supporting copy answering the three questions every visitor silently asks: what is this, is it for someone like me, and why should I believe it? The call to action: the measurable act, chosen deliberately from the evidence ladder — "join the waitlist" (email, weak but cheap), "get early access for 29 dollars" (money, strong), or a preorder with a stated ship date (strongest). The traffic source: strangers in the target segment, usually bought through search or social advertising, occasionally borrowed from relevant forums, newsletters or communities; never friends, whose clicks are worthless. And the counter: analytics that record visitors, clicks and completions so the result is a ratio, not an anecdote. Modern no-code site builders and payment links make the whole apparatus buildable in a day or two for well under a few hundred dollars, which is the point: the test should cost roughly a thousandth of what building the product would. Interpreting the ratio requires two honesty rules. First, define conversion against unique visitors from cold traffic only, and segment out anyone who arrived from your own network. Second, compare like with like: email-signup rates and paid-conversion rates live on different planets, and a 30 percent waitlist rate is weaker evidence than a 2 percent prepayment rate. As rough orientation for cold traffic: below roughly 5 percent email signup, the promise as worded is probably not landing; 10 to 30 percent suggests the problem resonates; for actual payment, low single digits can be excellent, since even mature e-commerce sites typically convert only 2 to 4 percent of visitors. Treat these as compass bearings, not laws — they swing with audience quality, price point and copywriting skill. The smoke test's great limitation is that it measures the appeal of a promise, not satisfaction with a product: it can tell you people want the outcome described, not that your eventual implementation will deliver it, retain them or earn referrals. Its great virtue is that it fails fast and in public, with strangers, before the expensive part begins — and a promise that cannot attract even emails from the very people it names is a verdict most builders can act on.

sections.heading: Buying Signal: Ad Experiments and the Arithmetic of a Test
sections.body: Because a smoke test needs strangers, paid advertising is usually its fuel, and the advertising layer is itself a demand instrument. Running small paid campaigns against a landing page yields three separate readings. The click-through rate — what fraction of people who saw the ad clicked it — measures whether the problem statement stops the scroll of the audience you claim to serve; on major social platforms, click-through rates around one half of one percent to one percent are typical, so materially beating one percent with a plain statement of the problem is an early sign of resonance, while rates far below that, in front of the right audience, suggest indifference no product will cure. The cost per click prices the attention of your market and feeds directly into unit economics. And conversion on the page, multiplied through, yields the number that decides ventures: customer acquisition cost. A worked example shows the arithmetic. Suppose you budget 300 dollars, and clicks cost 1.50 dollars on average: about 200 visitors. If 8 percent join the waitlist, an email lead costs 300 divided by 16, about 19 dollars. If instead you tested a 25-dollar preorder and 2 percent bought, each of the roughly 4 buyers cost 75 dollars to acquire against 25 dollars of revenue — which is not automatically bad news: ad-driven acquisition usually improves with optimization, and a subscription product recovers a 75-dollar acquisition cost in a few months of retention. The test's job is to surface this arithmetic before the product exists, so you learn whether the business model has to fight gravity. Practical craft keeps the readings clean. Run several ad variants — different problem framings, different audiences — with meaningful spend on each rather than one big undifferentiated blast, because the variant comparison is itself information about positioning; platforms' own split-testing tools handle the randomization. Send traffic to identical pages except for the one element under test. Let campaigns run a few days at least, since day-one performance is noisy and platforms need time to learn delivery. Expect and discount bot and accidental clicks, which inflate visits and deflate conversion; filtering to engaged visitors (those who scrolled or stayed beyond a few seconds) gives a fairer denominator. Mind the platform's grain: search ads capture people actively hunting for a solution, so they test demand among problem-aware customers; social ads interrupt people who were not searching, so they test whether the problem statement itself can create attention — a harder, and for genuinely new categories more relevant, exam. A few hundred dollars of ads cannot tell you your product will succeed. It can tell you, for less than the cost of a conference ticket, what strangers' attention costs, which framing of the problem earns it, and whether anyone follows through when asked to act — three numbers most founders historically discovered only after the engineering money was gone.

sections.heading: Wizard of Oz and Concierge Tests
sections.body: Some products cannot be judged from a landing page because their value lies in the experience of using them. For these, two closely related techniques let you sell and deliver the product before it exists, by secretly substituting human labor for the technology you have not built. In a Wizard of Oz test — named for the man behind the curtain — the customer sees what appears to be a finished, automated product, while behind the interface people do the work by hand. The canonical origin story is Zappos: in 1999 Nick Swinmurn wanted to know whether Americans would buy shoes online without trying them on, a proposition then widely considered absurd. Instead of building warehouses and inventory systems, he photographed shoes at local stores in San Francisco, posted the pictures on a simple website, and when an order arrived he walked to the store, bought the shoes at full retail price, and shipped them himself. Every transaction lost money and proved something: real strangers, paying real money, for the core proposition. Zappos grew into a company Amazon bought in 2009 for around 1.2 billion dollars, and the warehouses were built only after the demand was demonstrated. The concierge test drops the curtain: the customer knows a human is doing the work, because the human is standing next to them. Food on the Table, an Austin startup later acquired by Food Network's parent, began with its founder personally visiting families, planning their weekly meals around grocery-store sales, and charging roughly ten dollars a month for what would eventually become an app — the founder was the algorithm, and every session was simultaneously revenue, requirements-gathering and a retention experiment. The two techniques answer slightly different questions. Wizard of Oz tests whether customers will buy and use the product as it will eventually appear, and is well suited to testing automated services — a scheduling assistant, a recommendation engine — where the interface is the product. Concierge tests whether the underlying service creates enough value that customers pay and return, and is better early, when you still need to learn what the service should even be, since conversation is part of the method. Both share a decisive property: they generate top-of-ladder evidence — payment and repeat usage — while deferring nearly all engineering cost, and they surface operational surprises (what customers actually ask for, where quality fails) that no page test can. Both also share constraints to respect. They do not scale, by design; the point is learning per customer, not customers per month, and a handful of paying users served by hand teaches more than a thousand anonymous visitors. Unit economics will look terrible and should be ignored temporarily but modeled honestly: the question is whether software can eventually do what the human is doing at a cost the price supports. And where the customer is deceived about automation in ways that matter — privacy, safety, professional advice — the curtain must come down; a test that depends on the customer never finding out is a test of something other than demand.

sections.heading: Preorders, Deposits and Crowdfunding
sections.body: The strongest demand evidence available before a product exists is a completed purchase of it, and an entire commercial infrastructure now exists for collecting exactly that. Crowdfunding platforms are demand tests with a business model attached. When Pebble put its smartwatch on Kickstarter in April 2012 seeking 100,000 dollars, it raised 10.3 million from nearly 69,000 backers in 37 days — at that time the largest campaign in the platform's history — and the number did more than fund tooling: it proved, with money, a market that every venture investor had previously declined to believe in. The platform's all-or-nothing structure is itself good experimental design: backers are only charged if the goal is met, which lowers their risk of pledging, while the public running total creates a legible, timestamped demand curve. But crowdfunding's history also teaches the limits of the instrument. The Coolest Cooler raised 13.3 million dollars in 2014, then drowned in manufacturing reality, tariffs and unit economics, ultimately leaving roughly a third of backers without the product; demand was real, and the venture failed anyway, because a demand test validates the market, never the operations, margins or supply chain. Deposits are the same evidence in a quieter form. When Tesla opened 1,000-dollar refundable reservations for the Model 3 in March 2016, about 325,000 people paid within a week — roughly 14 billion dollars in implied future revenue — before any customer had driven the car. The deposit's genius is its calibrated cost: refundable, so the risk to the customer is only liquidity and attention, yet real enough that only genuine intenders pay. A startup can run the same play at any scale: a 50-dollar refundable deposit against a 500-dollar product, collected through an ordinary payment link, converts "I'd buy that" into a countable, reversible act. Honesty rules make the difference between a test and a trap. State plainly that the product is not finished and give your genuine ship estimate; delays are the norm in hardware — analyses of Kickstarter projects have found most deliver late — and buyers forgive delay far more readily than surprise. Offer refunds without friction, both because it is right and because a refund rate is itself data: preorders that quietly evaporate on request were curiosity, not demand. Account for the enthusiasm premium: crowdfunding audiences are early adopters who enjoy backing things, and campaign conversion overstates how the mass market will behave — a campaign that barely clears its goal on the strength of friends and a press bump may still have no durable market behind it. And never spend preorder money as if it were profit; it is inventory liability plus a message. Read as designed, a preorder test yields the three numbers that matter most: how many strangers paid, what acquiring each cost, and what fraction asked for their money back when reality's timeline appeared.

sections.heading: Fake Doors, Feature Stubs and the Ethics of Pretending
sections.body: Inside an existing product or store, demand testing gets even cheaper, because the audience is already present. The fake door test presents an entrance to a product or feature that does not yet exist — a menu item, a "Pro" tier button, an option on a pricing page, a shelf tag for a variant not yet made — and counts who tries to walk through. Clicks on the door measure demand in the most relevant population there is: your current users, in context, mid-task. Behind the door, the honest implementation matters: a short message saying the feature is coming, an invitation to leave an email to be notified, perhaps a one-question "what were you hoping this would do?" box, which converts a dead end into a signup and a requirements interview. Large software companies run such stubs constantly, and the same logic works physically — a restaurant can list a prospective dish and count orders before perfecting the recipe (apologizing and comping a dessert when it is ordered), a retailer can gauge interest in a product line with a display and a raincheck list. The measurement is clean: the click rate on the fake door, against the traffic that saw it, benchmarked against click rates of comparable real features, tells you whether demand clears the bar you set in advance. The technique's power is exactly why its ethics need stating. The currency being spent is user trust, and it is spent in small, cumulative amounts every time someone clicks and hits a wall. Guidelines that keep the account solvent: show the door to the smallest sample that yields a decision, not the whole user base; resolve the moment of disappointment immediately and gracefully — acknowledge, explain, offer notification, thank; never take payment through a fake door unless you are fully prepared to deliver or instantly refund with an apology; keep the test short-lived; and follow through with the people who signed up, who have effectively volunteered as your beta list. There are also places fake doors should not go. Testing fake safety features, fake medical or financial capabilities, or anything a user might rely on in a decision with real stakes is not a demand test but a deception with consequences. Regulated industries and advertising law constrain the outer edge as well: claiming an unavailable product is available for sale, as opposed to labeled as coming, can constitute false advertising. Handled within these lines, the fake door is among the highest signal-per-dollar instruments in the kit, because it samples real users at the real moment of need. It carries one systematic bias worth remembering: existing users are people who already chose you, so a fake door measures expansion demand within your franchise, not whether strangers would join it — for that, the landing page and the ad campaign remain the honest instruments.

sections.heading: Testing Price, Not Just Interest
sections.body: A demand test that never mentions price tests appetite for free things, which is nearly universal and nearly worthless. Price is not a detail to settle later; it is part of the product's identity and often the assumption most likely to be fatal, so it belongs inside the experiment. The gentlest instrument is the Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter, a 1976 survey technique that asks four questions about a described product: at what price would it be so expensive you would not consider it; at what price expensive but still worth considering; at what price a bargain; and at what price so cheap you would doubt its quality. Plotting the cumulative answers yields a range of acceptable prices and a rough optimal point. Because it is stated-preference data it inherits all the weaknesses of talk — people answering surveys spend imaginary money — but it is quick, cheap, and good at revealing the shape and width of a price band, especially whether customers even agree on what category of expense this is: answers scattered from five dollars to five hundred mean the product's reference class is unsettled, which is a positioning problem no price can fix. Behavioral instruments rank higher on the evidence ladder. The simplest is to put a price on the smoke test and vary it: run otherwise-identical landing pages at 9, 19 and 39 dollars to separate cold-traffic cohorts and compare not just conversion but revenue per visitor — it is routine for the higher price to win on revenue despite converting fewer, and the shape of the falloff sketches the demand curve. Willingness-to-pay auctions and preorder tiers add texture: offering early-bird, standard and premium tiers on a preorder page reveals how much of the audience self-selects upward, and the tier mix is a pricing experiment run with real money. For business products, the behavioral test is simply asking for the order at a stated price and watching the negotiation begin — the objection "that's more than we pay for X" is a gift, naming your true competitive anchor. Several cautions keep price tests honest. Differential pricing during tests can irritate customers who compare notes; keep test cells separated in time or audience, honor the lowest price shown to anyone who buys, and never charge two visible customers different prices for the same thing at the same moment without a stated reason (early-bird status is a stated reason). Beware the free-tier trap: measuring uptake of a free version tells you about distribution, not demand, and conversion from free to paid — historically in the low single digits of percent for consumer software — is the number that decides the business.
