The form persists because for the right situations it is genuinely efficient: two established professionals sharing an office and splitting fees, family members running a farm, a short-term joint undertaking between companies, which the law treats as a joint venture, essentially a partnership limited to a single project and governed by the same rules. It is the wrong form the moment strangers to each other's finances, meaningful assets, or outside investors enter the picture; every later section of this guide describes some upgrade, an agreement, an LLP registration, a conversion to an LLC, whose purpose is to keep the general partnership's flexibility while blunting its dangers.

sections.heading: Limited Partnerships: Two Classes of Partner
sections.body:
A limited partnership, abbreviated LP, splits ownership into two classes with radically different rights and risks. General partners run the business and remain personally liable for its obligations, exactly as in a general partnership. Limited partners are passive investors: they contribute capital, share in profits, and, in exchange for staying out of management, enjoy limited liability, meaning the most they can lose is their investment. Unlike a general partnership, an LP is a creature of statute and cannot arise by accident: it exists only when a certificate of limited partnership is filed with the state, typically naming the general partner and the registered agent, and the firm's name must usually contain the words limited partnership or the abbreviation LP. The governing statutes descend from the Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 1916, heavily revised in 1976 and 1985 and rewritten in 2001; Delaware's version, the Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act, dominates sophisticated practice because so many investment vehicles organize there.

Historically the limited partner's shield came with a sharp condition called the control rule: a limited partner who took part in control of the business risked being treated as a general partner, personally liable to creditors who reasonably believed they were dealing with one. Decades of litigation over what counted as control, voting on major decisions, advising the general partner, working for the firm, made the rule a trap, and statutes progressively defanged it with safe-harbor lists of permitted activities. The 2001 uniform act abolished the control rule outright, providing that a limited partner is not personally liable even if participating in management, and Delaware followed; in states retaining older acts, caution persists, and well-drafted agreements still channel limited partners' influence through defined consent rights, votes on enumerated major decisions, rather than day-to-day authority.

The LP's enduring importance is as the chassis of the investment-fund industry. Virtually every private equity fund, venture capital fund, hedge fund, and many real estate syndications are organized as limited partnerships: the fund manager, or an entity it controls, serves as general partner, and the investors, pension funds, endowments, wealthy individuals, are the limited partners. The economics made famous by this structure, a management fee of around two percent of committed capital plus carried interest of around twenty percent of profits above a hurdle, live in the limited partnership agreement, along with capital-call mechanics, distribution waterfalls, clawbacks, and the advisory-committee consents that substitute for limited-partner control. Because a general partner's unlimited liability would be intolerable for a fund manager, the general partner is almost always itself a limited-liability entity, an LLC or corporation, a doubling of structures that is standard practice and perfectly legal, though it means the LP form's personal liability has become, in this world, largely ceremonial. Some states also offer the limited liability limited partnership, or LLLP, which extends LLP-style protection to the general partner directly.

Two other habitats deserve mention. Family limited partnerships hold operating businesses, real estate, or portfolios for estate-planning purposes: senior family members serve as or control the general partner, gift limited interests to children over time, and, because minority, non-controlling interests are worth less per unit than the underlying assets, claim valuation discounts that reduce transfer taxes, a practice the IRS polices but courts have repeatedly sustained when the partnership has substance. And certain traditional businesses, real estate development, oil and gas, theatrical productions, still raise money through LPs because the form cleanly separates the promoter who bears the risk from investors who want a defined, capped exposure. Interests sold to passive investors are securities, so federal and state securities law, disclosure obligations and exemptions such as Regulation D, ride along with every LP offering.

sections.heading: Limited Liability Partnerships and Professional Firms
sections.body:
The limited liability partnership, or LLP, is the youngest of the partnership forms and was born from a specific catastrophe. After the savings-and-loan collapse of the late 1980s, regulators and receivers sued the law and accounting firms that had advised failed thrifts, and because those firms were general partnerships, every partner, including hundreds who had never touched the client, faced personal ruin for colleagues' alleged malpractice. Texas responded in 1991 with the first LLP statute, allowing a general partnership to register with the state and thereby shield innocent partners from liability for the errors of others, and the idea spread to every state within roughly a decade. The LLP is thus not a new kind of entity but a cloak over a general partnership: internally it is governed by ordinary partnership law and its own agreement; externally, registration changes who can be made to pay.

The core of the protection is the same everywhere: a partner in an LLP is not personally liable for the malpractice, negligence, or misconduct of other partners or of employees the partner did not supervise. Everyone remains fully liable for their own wrongdoing, registration is not a license for carelessness, and the firm's own assets are always on the line, which is why professional firms carry substantial malpractice insurance regardless of form, and why many states condition LLP status on maintaining minimum insurance or segregated funds. States historically split over how far the shield reached. Partial-shield statutes, the early Texas model, protected partners only from liability arising from others' errors and omissions, leaving them personally liable for the firm's ordinary contract debts, the lease, the bank loan. Full-shield statutes, now the strong majority position and the rule under RUPA's 1997 LLP provisions, protect partners from all partnership obligations, tort and contract alike, making the LLP's shield functionally similar to an LLC's. In practice the distinction is blunted by the market: landlords and lenders to professional firms routinely demand personal guarantees from partners, which waive the shield by contract for that creditor.

Mechanically, becoming an LLP is simple: the partnership files a registration or statement of qualification with the state, pays a fee, adds the required designation, LLP or Registered Limited Liability Partnership, to its name, and in most states renews annually. Some states restrict the form: California, notably, limits LLPs to specified professions, principally lawyers, accountants, and architects, while most states allow any business to register. The form's natural constituency remains the professions, partly for regulatory reasons, since some licensing bodies long forbade professionals to practice in corporations or LLCs, and partly for cultural ones, since partner remains the title the professions organize careers around. The result is visible at the top of the market: the Big Four accounting networks and the large law firms of the United States and the United Kingdom, where a 2000 statute created a distinct LLP entity with its own filing and disclosure regime, are overwhelmingly LLPs.

For taxes, an LLP is simply a partnership: profits pass through to partners, who typically pay self-employment taxes as active professionals. For governance, everything in this guide about agreements, capital accounts, fiduciary duties, and buyouts applies unchanged; large professional LLPs elaborate the machinery with executive committees, managing partners, compensation committees, and multi-tier partner classes, including the modern income partner or non-equity partner, who carries the title without a capital stake. The LLP's lesson in miniature is the theme of this whole guide: partnership law is a set of defaults, and the forms differ chiefly in one question, when things go wrong, whose personal assets answer for it.

sections.heading: The Partnership Agreement
sections.body:
A partnership can exist without any written agreement, and that is precisely the problem: in the silence, the statute governs, and the statute's defaults, equal management votes, equal profit shares regardless of capital, no pay for work, unanimity for new partners, dissolution mechanics nobody has read, fit almost no real business. The partnership agreement is the document that replaces those defaults with the deal the partners actually intend, and under RUPA it is king: with a short list of exceptions, relations among the partners and between the partners and the partnership are governed by the partnership agreement, and the statute applies only where the agreement is silent. Courts routinely enforce harsh but clear terms against partners who later regret them, which cuts both ways: the agreement will protect you exactly to the extent you thought it through.

A competent agreement answers, at minimum, the following questions. Identity and purpose: who the partners are, the firm's name, its business, and its intended duration, a fixed term, a particular undertaking, or at will. Money in: each partner's initial contribution of cash, property, or services, how contributions are valued, whether and how additional capital can be called, and what happens to a partner who fails to meet a call, dilution, forced loan treatment, or default remedies. Money out: how profits and losses are allocated, whether any partner receives guaranteed payments for working, how and when cash is distributed versus retained, and how draws are trued up against year-end results. Control: who manages day to day, which decisions require a majority, a supermajority, or unanimity, hiring, borrowing above a threshold, admitting partners, selling major assets, how votes are weighted, whether there is a managing partner or committee, and how deadlocks are broken, by a casting vote, a rotating tiebreaker, mediation, or a buyout mechanism. Change: how new partners are admitted and on what terms, what events trigger a partner's exit, death, disability, retirement, expulsion for cause, voluntary withdrawal, and, most important of any clause in the document, how a departing partner's interest is valued and paid for, the buy-sell machinery treated in its own section later. Endgame: what dissolves the firm, who winds up, and the order of payouts. Housekeeping: fiscal year, accounting method, banking, records access, dispute resolution, mediation or arbitration and where, amendment procedure, and any restrictive covenants such as confidentiality or non-solicitation, drafted with the caveat that non-competes face increasing legal limits in many states.

The law places a few floors under all this. Under RUPA, the agreement cannot eliminate the duty of loyalty or the obligation of good faith and fair dealing, though it can define categories of permitted conduct if not manifestly unreasonable; it cannot unreasonably restrict a partner's access to books and records; and it cannot strip a court's power in listed respects. Oral and even implied agreements are valid, partnership law has no general writing requirement, but proving the terms of a handshake years later, after memories have diverged along with interests, is litigation's bread and butter, and any term that cannot be performed within a year may run into the statute of frauds besides. The professional advice is uniform and worth its cost: write the agreement while everyone still likes each other, have a lawyer who represents the partnership, not one partner, draft or review it, make every partner take independent advice on the exit provisions, and revisit the document when anything material changes, a new partner, a big capital infusion, a partner's divorce or illness, because the agreement you need is the one in force the day something goes wrong.

sections.heading: Capital Contributions, Ownership, and Capital Accounts
sections.body:
Capital is what partners put at risk in the venture, and partnership accounting tracks it through a device every partner should understand: the capital account. Each partner has one. It begins with the value of what the partner contributed, cash at face value, property at its agreed fair market value, and thereafter it rises with the partner's share of profits and any further contributions, and falls with the partner's share of losses and any distributions taken out. At any moment, a partner's capital account states that partner's equity stake in the firm's books, and at dissolution, after creditors are paid, positive capital accounts are what the remaining cash is used to repay. The discipline of maintaining these accounts properly, in practice inside the firm's accounting software and formally on each year's tax return, is not bureaucratic fuss; it is the ledger from which buyouts, new admissions, and final settlements are computed, and sloppy capital accounting is a reliable source of partner litigation.

Contributions come in three flavors, each with its own wrinkles. Cash is simple. Property, equipment, real estate, intellectual property, a book of business, must be valued by agreement, and its tax treatment is distinctive: contributing appreciated property to a partnership is generally not a taxable event, the partnership takes the contributor's old basis, and the built-in gain is later allocated back to the contributor under section 704(c) of the tax code, a rule that prevents shifting one partner's latent tax bill onto the others. Services are the hard case. A partner who receives a capital interest, a present stake in the firm's existing value, in exchange for work has taxable compensation income at that value, immediately, in cash the partner may not have; the standard workaround is a profits interest, a stake only in future profits and appreciation, which under long-standing IRS guidance is generally not taxed at grant. Sweat-equity deals that ignore this distinction create ugly April surprises.

Ownership percentage, profit share, and capital account are three different numbers that beginners conflate. Partners may agree, for example, that one who contributed ninety percent of the capital holds a sixty percent profit share, in recognition of the other's full-time labor; or that profits split evenly while capital, and therefore liquidation proceeds, remain proportional to contributions. Partnership law permits nearly any arrangement, which is precisely why the agreement must state each partner's contribution, percentage interest, and profit share explicitly rather than leaving them to inference. Additional capital is its own negotiation: the agreement should say whether the firm can call for more money, by what vote, and what happens to a partner who cannot or will not pay, with the common answers being dilution by formula, treatment of other partners' cover as a loan bearing interest, or, in harsher documents, forfeiture remedies.

Two boundary lines complete the picture. A partner's loan to the partnership is not a contribution: it belongs on the books as debt, documented with a note and interest, and in winding up it is repaid ahead of capital, so mislabeling can cost real money. And distributions are not salary: routine cash taken by partners during the year, called draws, are advances against the year's profit share, reconciled at year end, while a fixed payment to a working partner regardless of profits is, in tax language, a guaranteed payment, deductible by the firm and ordinary income to the recipient. A capital account can go negative when losses and draws outrun contributions and profits, and whether a partner must restore that deficit at the end, or the shortfall falls on the others, is exactly the kind of question a good agreement answers in advance and a bad one leaves to a judge.

sections.heading: Pass-Through Taxation and the Schedule K-1
sections.body:
The single biggest financial fact about partnerships is that, for federal income tax, the partnership itself pays nothing. It is a pass-through: the firm computes its income, but the tax is levied on the partners, each taking their allocated share onto their own returns. The mechanics run through two documents. The partnership files Form 1065, an information return due the fifteenth day of the third month after year end, March 15 for calendar-year firms, reporting the firm's income, deductions, and each partner's share. Each partner then receives a Schedule K-1, the tax slip of partnership life, itemizing that partner's allocations, ordinary business income, rental income, interest, dividends, capital gains, charitable contributions, and more, each category keeping its character as it passes through, so a long-term capital gain at the firm level is a long-term capital gain on the partner's return. Partners attach nothing but report everything, and because K-1s often arrive late, partners of complex firms live on filing extensions.

Two features of this regime startle newcomers. First, phantom income: partners are taxed on their allocated share of profits whether or not any cash was distributed. A firm that earns 300,000 dollars and retains every cent for expansion still generates taxable income of 100,000 for each of three equal partners, who must find the tax from their own pockets, which is why well-run partnerships adopt a tax-distribution policy, distributing at least enough each year to cover partners' tax on allocated income. Second, no withholding: nobody deducts tax from a partner's draw, so partners must pay quarterly estimated taxes themselves, and the first year's surprise underpayment penalty is a rite of passage the K-1 does not warn you about.

Self-employment tax adds a second layer. A general partner's share of the firm's trade-or-business income, plus any guaranteed payments, is self-employment income, bearing the combined Social Security and Medicare tax of 15.3 percent up to the annually adjusted Social Security wage base and 2.9 percent, plus the 0.9 percent additional Medicare tax at high incomes, above it. Limited partners, by statute, exclude their distributive share from self-employment income, paying it only on guaranteed payments for services, and the proper treatment of LLC members and LLP partners who work in the business has been contested territory for years, with the IRS and courts increasingly looking at actual activity rather than the label. Working partners also cannot be their own W-2 employees; their compensation is guaranteed payments, and their health insurance and retirement contributions flow through special K-1 and personal-return channels rather than payroll.

The regime's great luxury is flexibility. Unlike an S corporation, which must allocate everything strictly by share ownership, a partnership may make special allocations, directing depreciation deductions to the money partner, front-loading losses to whoever can use them, provided the allocation has substantial economic effect under the section 704(b) regulations, which in essence require that capital accounts be properly maintained and that tax allocations track real economic benefit and burden. Losses a partner is allocated are deductible only up to the partner's basis in the partnership interest, and further limited by the at-risk and passive-activity rules, so paper losses do not automatically shelter other income. Since 2018, audits happen at the partnership level under the centralized partnership audit regime created by the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015, with any adjustment collectible from the firm itself unless it elects to push the adjustment out to the partners, an arcane but consequential choice every agreement should address by naming a partnership representative and specifying the election. State taxes vary widely, from nothing to entity-level franchise fees to mandatory withholding for out-of-state partners, and many states now offer elective pass-through entity taxes as a workaround to the federal cap on state tax deductions. None of this is do-it-yourself territory; a partnership's accountant earns the fee every March.

sections.heading: Splitting Profits, Losses, and Draws
sections.body:
How to split the money is the first question partners argue about and the last one many of them settle properly. The legal default, recall, is equal shares regardless of contribution, so any other intention must be written down. The design space is wide, and real firms use all of it. Proportional-to-capital splits suit ventures where money is the scarce input: three investors funding a building at 50-30-20 take profits 50-30-20. Equal splits suit genuine peers contributing similar work and cash. Hybrid formulas handle the common asymmetry of one partner with money and another with time: a preferred return, say eight percent annually on contributed capital, paid first, with remaining profits split by an agreed ratio that honors labor; or a salary-like guaranteed payment to the working partner off the top, with the true profit split proportional to capital afterward. Professional firms elaborate endlessly: lockstep systems, classically used by elite law firms, advance every partner's share with seniority in fixed steps, buying cohesion at the cost of rewarding rainmakers; eat-what-you-kill systems allocate by collections a partner originates, sharpening incentives and corroding collaboration; most firms land between, with compensation committees weighing origination, hours, management, and mentoring. The scheme is not merely arithmetic, it is the firm's incentive system, and misaligned splits are the leading root cause of partnership breakups.

Whatever the formula, the agreement should separate three flows that beginners blur. Allocation is the bookkeeping and tax assignment of the year's profit or loss to each partner's capital account and K-1; it happens whether or not cash moves. Distribution is cash actually paid out, on whatever schedule the agreement or the partners' vote sets, and prudent firms retain part of profits as working capital, distributing the rest after the books close. Draws are periodic advances, monthly or weekly checks that let partners live during the year, debited against the capital account and trued up when the year's profit is known; a partner whose draws exceeded the final share owes the difference back or carries a reduced account. Confusing a draw with a salary leads partners to overspend retained profits; confusing allocation with distribution leads them to be shocked by tax on money they never received, the phantom-income problem of the previous section, best solved by a standing tax-distribution clause.

Losses deserve equal drafting attention, because sharing pain is harder than sharing gain. By default losses follow profit shares, but partners can agree otherwise, subject to the tax rules on substantial economic effect and to the practical point that a loss allocation is only worth something to a partner with basis and outside income to absorb it. The agreement should say whether partners must contribute additional funds to cover operating shortfalls, capital calls, or whether the firm borrows, and what happens to a partner who cannot pay a call. In leveraged ventures, the interaction of debt, loss allocations, and negative capital accounts is exactly where amateur drafting collapses; the money partner's lawyer will insist on provisions, qualified income offsets, minimum-gain chargebacks, whose names alone signal that a professional wrote the document.

Two pieces of housekeeping keep the peace. First, transparency: every partner should receive the same financial statements, and the agreement should guarantee access to books and records, which the law protects anyway. Second, revision: splits set at founding rarely fit year five, when one partner's role has grown and another's has shrunk. Well-run firms schedule a periodic compensation review, annually or biennially, with a defined process, rather than waiting for resentment to force a renegotiation under threat. A split renegotiated calmly on schedule is a business decision; the same conversation held mid-crisis is a dissolution rehearsal.

sections.heading: Management, Voting, and the Power to Bind the Firm
sections.body:
Partnership governance rests on a default so egalitarian it startles corporate people: absent contrary agreement, every partner has an equal say in the business, one vote each, regardless of capital, and ordinary matters are decided by a majority of partners. Only matters outside the ordinary course, and amendments to the partnership agreement itself, require unanimous consent under the default rule. In a two-partner firm this means every disputed ordinary decision is a deadlock, and in any firm it means the ninety-percent capital partner can be outvoted by two ten-percent partners, results almost nobody intends, which is why the management article of the agreement matters as much as the money articles. Standard redesigns include weighting votes by percentage interest; designating a managing partner with defined day-to-day authority and a defined leash, spending limits, hiring authority, reporting duties; creating an executive committee in larger firms, elected on a stated cycle; and building a tiered consent schedule, ordinary operations to the manager, significant matters, borrowing over a threshold, leases, litigation, budgets, to a majority or supermajority, and fundamental matters, admitting partners, selling the business, amending the agreement, merging, to unanimity or near-unanimity. Deadlock machinery belongs here too, especially in fifty-fifty firms: escalation to mediation, a neutral tie-breaking director for defined questions, or, as the last resort, a buyout trigger such as the shotgun clause described in the buy-sell section.

Separate from how partners decide internally is what any single partner can do to outsiders, and here partnership law contains its most dangerous feature. Every partner is an agent of the partnership for the purpose of its business: an act of a partner apparently carrying on the partnership's ordinary business binds the firm, even if the partner had no actual authority, even if the partners had expressly voted the act down, unless the third party knew or had received notice that the partner lacked authority. The doctrine, apparent authority, protects commerce, outsiders cannot audit a firm's internal politics before accepting an order, and it means internal restrictions are only as good as the world's knowledge of them. If the agreement forbids any single partner to sign contracts above twenty-five thousand dollars, but a partner signs a fifty-thousand-dollar deal with a vendor who knew nothing of the limit, the firm is bound, and every partner's personal assets stand behind it; the firm's recourse is an internal claim against the overstepping partner. Acts outside the ordinary course, selling the firm's building, guaranteeing a stranger's debt, do not bind without actual authority, and RUPA lets a partnership file an optional statement of partnership authority with the state, useful chiefly for real estate, where recorded limits on who may convey property bind the world.

Beyond votes and agency, partners hold statutory information rights the agreement cannot unreasonably cut off: access to the books and records, and a right to information concerning the partnership's business reasonably required for the proper exercise of a partner's rights. Sound firms institutionalize this rather than merely permitting it: regular partner meetings with minutes, annual budgets adopted by vote, financial statements delivered on a schedule, and written consents documenting major decisions. The documentation habit has three payoffs. It prevents the who-agreed-to-what disputes that fuel partner litigation; it evidences the ordinary-course boundaries that define each partner's apparent authority; and it builds the record of fair process that matters enormously if a decision is later attacked as a breach of fiduciary duty, the subject of the next section. Governance, in a partnership, is not overhead; it is the difference between co-owners and co-defendants.

sections.heading: Liability: What Partners Risk
sections.body:
The defining risk of the general partnership form is stated in one sentence of the statute: all partners are liable jointly and severally for all obligations of the partnership. Unpack the phrase and its weight becomes clear. Jointly and severally means a creditor with a judgment may collect the entire amount from any one partner, at the creditor's choice, not merely each partner's proportionate slice; the partner who pays is left to seek contribution from the others, a right that is worthless if they are insolvent or gone. All obligations means everything: contracts the firm signed, loans it took, damages for a partner's or employee's negligence committed in the ordinary course of business, even liabilities the complaining partner personally opposed and voted against. The exposure is unlimited, reaching a partner's personal savings, investments, and, subject to state exemptions, home. Under RUPA, a creditor must generally exhaust the partnership's own assets before levying on a partner's personal property, an entity-first rule that softens procedure but not substance, and a person admitted to an existing partnership is not personally liable for obligations incurred before admission, though the capital they contributed stands behind old debts. Departure does not erase exposure either: a partner remains liable for obligations incurred while a partner, unless creditors agree to a release, and can even be bound by post-departure dealings with counterparties who reasonably still believed the person a partner, which is why RUPA provides a filed statement of dissociation that cuts off such lingering liability ninety days after filing, and why lawyers send notice letters to every significant creditor and customer when a partner leaves.

Against this backdrop, the liability geography of the other forms is best understood as a map of exceptions. In a limited partnership, only the general partner bears unlimited liability; limited partners risk their investment. In an LLP, partners are shielded from liability for the firm's obligations, in full-shield states both tort and contract, but never from their own malpractice or wrongdoing, and never from obligations they personally guaranteed. In an LLC or corporation, owners as such are not liable for entity debts at all. Yet in the small-business world these shields leak by consent: banks, landlords, and major suppliers routinely require personal guarantees from the owners of small entities regardless of form, so the practical liability question is often not what the statute says but what the lease says. Shields also fail for personal fault, the professional who commits the malpractice, the driver who causes the crash, and for certain statutory liabilities, unpaid payroll withholding taxes above all, which the tax code collects personally from responsible persons of any entity.

Risk management therefore proceeds on three fronts at once. Structure: do not operate a business with meaningful liability exposure as a bare general partnership; register as an LLP or organize as an LLC, and when an LP is used, make the general partner an entity. Insurance: general commercial liability, professional liability for advice-giving businesses, commercial auto, workers' compensation where there are employees, and umbrella coverage sized to the realistic worst case; insurance, not entity form, is what actually pays most claims. Discipline: keep the firm's finances rigorously separate from personal accounts, document decisions, and avoid the informal commingling that invites courts to disregard the entity. Finally, understand the reverse direction: a partner's personal creditors cannot seize partnership assets or force their way into management; their remedy is a charging order against the debtor-partner's distributions, a feature that makes partnership-taxed entities useful in asset-protection planning. Liability, in short, is the axis around which the entire choice-of-form decision described later in this guide revolves.

sections.heading: Fiduciary Duties Between Partners
sections.body:
Partners do not deal with each other at arm's length. The law makes each partner a fiduciary of the partnership and, through it, of the other partners, holding them to a standard famously stated by Judge Benjamin Cardozo in Meinhard v. Salmon, a 1928 New York case that remains the most quoted passage in American partnership law. Salmon, managing a hotel venture funded half by Meinhard, quietly took for himself a lucrative new lease on the property as the venture neared its end; the court gave Meinhard his share, and Cardozo wrote that joint adventurers owe one another the duty of the finest loyalty, that many forms of conduct permissible in a workaday world for those acting at arm's length are forbidden to those bound by fiduciary ties, and that the standard is not honesty alone, but the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive. The rhetoric has teeth: its practical meaning is that a partner may not secretly take for personal benefit what belongs, even arguably, to the common enterprise.

Modern statutes organize the obligation into named duties. The duty of loyalty has three statutory branches under RUPA: to account to the partnership for any benefit derived from partnership business or from use of partnership property, including the appropriation of a partnership opportunity; to refrain from self-dealing, that is, acting as or for a party with an interest adverse to the partnership in its transactions; and to refrain from competing with the partnership before dissolution. The classic violations are timeless: diverting a customer or deal to a side company, buying the building the firm rents and raising its rent, taking kickbacks from suppliers, using firm staff and funds for a personal project, or exploiting information learned through the firm. The duty of care is gentler, requiring partners to refrain from grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or knowing violations of law; ordinary bad judgment, honestly exercised, is not actionable, a partnership cousin of the business-judgment rule. Alongside both runs the obligation of good faith and fair dealing in exercising rights under the agreement, and a duty of candor in practice: partners must volunteer material information about the business, and the statute guarantees access to books and records. Remedies for breach include damages, disgorgement of the wrongful gain, a formal accounting, expulsion where the agreement permits, and, in egregious cases, judicial dissolution.

The duties are default rules with limited adjustability, and the limits matter. RUPA forbids eliminating the duty of loyalty or the good-faith obligation, but permits the agreement to identify specific types or categories of activities that do not violate the duty of loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable, and to authorize partners to ratify a particular conflicted transaction after full disclosure. Sophisticated agreements use this room deliberately: real estate partners commonly waive claims to each other's separate projects, venture funds define what opportunities belong to the fund, and family partnerships bless dealings with affiliated entities, all enforceable because they are specific and informed rather than blanket absolutions. Delaware's statutes go further, allowing broad elimination of fiduciary duties in limited partnerships and LLCs by clear contract, which is one reason institutional deals concentrate there, though even Delaware preserves the implied covenant of good faith.

For working partners the operational rules are simple to state and demanding to live. Disclose every conflict before acting, in writing, and let the disinterested partners decide. Treat firm opportunities as the firm's until the partners, informed, release them. Paper related-party transactions at demonstrable market terms. Never use firm money, staff, or information for outside benefit without consent. And when leaving, remember the duties persist through winding up: departing partners have been held liable for soliciting firm clients and poaching staff while still partners. The fiduciary standard is the legal expression of what a partnership is socially, a relationship of trust, and courts enforce the trust more strictly than any other term of the deal.

sections.heading: Adding Partners, Exits, and Buy-Sell Agreements
sections.body:
Partnerships change shape over their lives, and the machinery for admitting and removing partners is where good drafting pays its largest dividends. Admission first. The statutory default requires unanimous consent of the existing partners to admit a new one, a rule the agreement can relax to a supermajority or delegate to a committee. The economic mechanics need equal care: does the incoming partner buy in with cash, contribute property, or earn in over time; does the buy-in purchase a slice of existing value, which is taxable richness for the sellers, or only a share of future profits, the profits-interest route common for promoted employees; and does the newcomer's admission dilute everyone proportionally or come out of one retiring partner's share? Professional firms formalize all of this into partner tracks, with income-partner stages, capital buy-ins often financed by bank loans arranged by the firm, and vesting schedules. Whatever the design, the admission documents should include the new partner's signature joining the partnership agreement, because a partner not bound by the agreement is governed by the statutory defaults, and no one wants a two-regime firm.

Exits are the hard half, and the law's baseline is now the RUPA concept of dissociation: a partner can leave, by choice, death, bankruptcy, expulsion, or other listed events, without automatically destroying the firm. Unless the departure triggers dissolution under the agreement or statute, the partnership continues and must buy out the dissociated partner's interest at a statutorily defined buyout price, essentially the partner's share of the greater of liquidation value or going-concern value, with interest, litigated valuation being the default's built-in flaw. A partner who quits in breach of an agreed term leaves wrongfully and owes damages, which can be netted against the buyout. Expulsion, the firm removing a partner, exists by default only in narrow judicial forms; if the partners want the practical power to remove someone, for cause or without cause, the agreement must create it, define the vote required, and fix the price, and courts enforce such clauses while policing bad-faith expulsions aimed at seizing a partner's book of business.

Because the statutory buyout is a lawsuit waiting to happen, well-advised firms replace it wholesale with a buy-sell agreement, either inside the partnership agreement or as a companion document. A complete buy-sell answers four questions for every trigger event, death, permanent disability, retirement, voluntary withdrawal, expulsion, personal bankruptcy, and, in many firms, a partner's divorce, so that a stranger or an estate never becomes an unwanted co-owner. Who buys: the entity itself, a redemption, or the remaining partners individually, a cross-purchase, a choice with real tax and basis consequences. At what price: a fixed price refreshed annually in a signed certificate, a formula such as a multiple of average earnings or adjusted book value, or a professional appraisal, ideally one appraiser chosen jointly, with a baseball-arbitration fallback; stale fixed prices are the classic malpractice. Paid how: life insurance funds death buyouts cheaply, each partner insuring the others in a cross-purchase or the firm insuring all in a redemption; lifetime buyouts are typically installment notes over three to seven years with interest and security, sized so the payout does not strangle the survivor firm's cash flow. And with what protections: rights of first refusal on any attempted transfer, automatic conversion of a transferee to a mere economic-interest holder with no management rights, and non-solicitation covenants from the departing partner. Two colorful mechanisms deserve mention: the shotgun clause, under which one partner names a price and the other must either buy or sell at it, elegantly self-policing but dangerous when wealth is unequal, since the richer partner can name a low price the poorer one cannot afford to accept as buyer; and drag-along and tag-along rights borrowed from corporate practice for whole-firm sales. The test of a buy-sell is simple: read it imagining each partner dead, disabled, divorced, or furious, and see whether the document answers every question without a negotiation.

sections.heading: Disputes, Deadlock, Dissociation, and Dissolution
sections.body:
Partnership disputes have a small number of root causes, money, workload, direction, and trust, and a predictable escalation path, which means the machinery for handling them can be designed in advance. The first line is structural prevention: clear splits reviewed on schedule, documented decisions, financial transparency, and defined roles, the hygiene described throughout this guide. The second line is contractual process. A good agreement prescribes an escalation ladder for disagreements: direct negotiation between partners, then mediation before a neutral, which settles a large share of business disputes cheaply and preserves relationships, then binding arbitration or litigation as the terminus, with the choice made deliberately, arbitration for privacy and speed, courts for appellate rights and injunctions, and the clause specifying seat, rules, and who pays. Deadlock in evenly divided firms deserves its own device, a rotating casting vote, a standing neutral, or a buyout trigger, because a fifty-fifty firm with no tiebreaker has a constitutional crisis latent in every serious disagreement.

When a particular partner is the problem, the modern framework channels the response through dissociation rather than destruction. Under RUPA, dissociation events include a partner's express will to withdraw, events specified in the agreement, expulsion pursuant to the agreement, judicial expulsion for wrongful conduct or material breach, bankruptcy, incapacity, and death. Dissociation forks into two paths. On the continuation path, the firm survives, the dissociated partner's interest is purchased under the buyout rules or, far better, the buy-sell machinery of the previous section, and the departed partner's lingering apparent authority and liability are extinguished by notice and by filing a statement of dissociation, effective against the world ninety days after filing. On the winding-up path, the departure is one of the events that dissolves the firm.

Dissolution is the legal beginning of the end, not the end itself. Its triggers, beyond those the agreement specifies, include the expiration of an agreed term or completion of the undertaking, unanimous consent, an event making the business unlawful, and judicial decree on grounds such as economic frustration, a partner's conduct making the business impracticable, or, in an at-will partnership, simply a partner's decision to leave, since an at-will firm dissolves by default when any partner expresses the will to withdraw, one more reason to give the firm a defined term or continuation clause. Dissolution is followed by winding up: the firm completes or assigns work in progress, collects receivables, liquidates or distributes assets, and pays claims in the statutory order, first to creditors, including partners who are creditors by virtue of documented loans, then to partners in settlement of their capital accounts, with any remaining surplus distributed as profits. If assets fall short, partners must contribute to cover the deficiency in their loss-sharing ratios, the final bite of unlimited liability, and a partner with a negative capital account may owe money into the pot rather than taking any out. Practicalities matter as much as the ledger: written notice to customers, suppliers, and lenders both preserves goodwill and cuts off apparent authority; registrations, licenses, and assumed names are cancelled; a statement of dissolution can be filed; final tax returns are marked final, with K-1s closing out each partner's basis; and records are retained for the statutory limitation periods. Partners winding up remain fiduciaries to the end, and the last act of many failed partnerships, the fight over the final accounting, is best prevented by the same tools that would have prevented the first fight: clean books, clear agreement, and a process everyone signed while they were still friends.

sections.heading: Partnership vs. LLC vs. Corporation
sections.body:
Choosing a business form is really answering four questions at once: who is liable, how is it taxed, how flexible is the governance, and what do investors and regulators expect. The partnership family answers them one way, the limited liability company another, and the corporation a third, and the modern verdict is worth stating up front: for most new multi-owner small businesses, the LLC taxed as a partnership has become the default choice, because it pairs the partnership's tax treatment and contractual freedom with corporate-grade liability protection. Wyoming created the LLC in 1977, the IRS blessed partnership taxation for it in 1988, every state had a statute by 1996, and the 1997 check-the-box regulations let any unincorporated entity simply elect its tax classification, which ended decades of formalistic gamesmanship. An LLC's owners, called members, are not personally liable for entity debts; its constitution, the operating agreement, is as freely drafted as any partnership agreement; and a multi-member LLC files the same Form 1065 and issues the same K-1s described earlier. Nearly everything in this guide about agreements, capital accounts, allocations, fiduciary duties, and buy-sell machinery applies to a multi-member LLC with the words changed, member for partner, operating agreement for partnership agreement, which is precisely why partnership law remains essential knowledge even as bare general partnerships fade.

Where do true partnerships still win? Professional practice, where licensing rules and tradition keep law and accounting firms in LLPs. Investment funds, where the limited partnership's GP-LP architecture, Delaware's contract-freedom statutes, and decades of precedent make the LP unbeatable. Situations prizing zero formation cost or ephemerality, short joint ventures between established companies. And any deal needing maximal tax flexibility with sophisticated counsel, though an LLC taxed as a partnership can do virtually everything an LP can. Conversely, the corporation wins on different ground. A C corporation is a separate taxpayer, paying the flat 21 percent federal rate set by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, with shareholders taxed again on dividends, the famous double tax, tolerable when profits are reinvested rather than distributed and sweetened by the qualified small business stock exclusion of section 1202, which can make gain on qualifying C-corporation stock tax-free up to large limits after a five-year hold. Venture capital effectively requires it: institutional investors want preferred stock, option pools, and no K-1s flowing to their own tax-exempt partners, so startups seeking VC organize as Delaware C corporations almost without exception. The S corporation, a tax election available to corporations and to LLCs, offers pass-through taxation with corporate rigidity, at most 100 shareholders, all U.S. individuals or qualifying trusts, one class of stock, strictly pro-rata distributions, and its enduring appeal is payroll-tax arithmetic: owner-operators pay themselves a reasonable W-2 salary bearing employment taxes, and take remaining profits as distributions free of self-employment tax, a structure the IRS polices for unreasonably low salaries but which saves real money for profitable service businesses.

A compressed decision guide, not a substitute for advice: solo owner, single-member LLC. Multi-owner operating business, LLC taxed as a partnership, considering an S election once profits comfortably exceed fair salaries. Licensed professionals, LLP or the state's professional entity. Raising venture capital, Delaware C corporation. Private fund or syndication, Delaware LP with an entity general partner. Bare general partnership, only for trivially low-risk collaborations, and even then, write the agreement. Conversions between forms are routine, statutory mergers and conversions exist in most states, but they carry tax consequences, especially leaving partnership taxation for corporate form or vice versa, so the cheapest structure is the one chosen correctly at the start.

sections.heading: Setting Up a Partnership: Registration, Banking, Insurance, and Records
sections.body:
The practical launch of a partnership is a checklist, and working it in order prevents most first-year misery. Everything begins before any form is filed, with the choice of partner, the highest-stakes decision in the whole enterprise. Partners are mutual agents with claims on each other's assets, so due diligence is not cynicism but respect: talk candidly about money habits, debts, credit, litigation history, family obligations, working hours, risk tolerance, and five-year intentions, and verify what can be verified. Many advisers suggest a trial project before any binding commitment. Then negotiate the partnership agreement while goodwill is high, using the checklist from the agreement section of this guide, with a lawyer drafting for the partnership and each partner separately advised on the exit and buyout terms; pair it with the buy-sell machinery and, where insurance will fund death buyouts, medical underwriting started early.

The governmental layer follows. A general partnership needs no formation filing, but an LP files its certificate of limited partnership and an LLP its registration or statement of qualification with the secretary of state, and any partnership operating under a name other than the partners' surnames registers that assumed or fictitious name, the DBA, with the state or county, sometimes with newspaper publication. Obtain the federal Employer Identification Number, free and immediate on the IRS website, because banks require it and the Form 1065 will be filed under it. Check state and local business licenses, professional licenses, sales-tax registration if selling taxable goods, and employer registrations, unemployment insurance and withholding accounts, if hiring. Then build the financial spine: a dedicated partnership bank account funded by the initial contributions, with the signature authority the agreement specifies, and absolute separation from personal finances, commingling being both an accounting nightmare and the classic bad fact in liability litigation. Stand up bookkeeping from day one, cash or accrual method chosen with the accountant, a chart of accounts that tracks each partner's capital account, contributions, draws, and allocations, and a document folder holding the agreement, filings, EIN letter, licenses, insurance policies, and major contracts.

Insurance converts the liability chapter of this guide into premiums: general commercial liability for premises and operations, professional liability for advice-giving businesses, commercial property, commercial auto for business vehicles, workers' compensation where required by employees, cyber coverage where client data lives, umbrella coverage sized to a realistic worst case, and the life and disability policies that fund the buy-sell. Finally, install the operating rhythms that keep partnerships healthy: draws on a schedule with a year-end true-up, quarterly estimated-tax reminders for every partner, a tax-distribution policy, financial statements shared monthly, a standing partner meeting with minutes, the Form 1065 calendared for March 15 with K-1s to partners, and an annual review of the agreement, insurance limits, and buy-sell valuation certificate. None of these steps is difficult; their absence, multiplied by time and money, is where partnerships go to die.
steps: Vet your prospective partners thoroughly: discuss finances, debts, credit, work habits, risk tolerance, and long-term goals, and verify claims where possible before committing.

Negotiate and sign a written partnership agreement covering contributions, ownership, profit and loss splits, draws, management votes, admission, exits, buyout valuation, dispute resolution, and dissolution, with independent legal advice on exit terms.
Choose and register the business name, filing a DBA or assumed-name certificate if the firm operates under anything other than the partners' own names.

File the required state formation documents for the chosen form: certificate of limited partnership for an LP, or LLP registration or statement of qualification for an LLP; a general partnership files none.
Obtain a federal Employer Identification Number from the IRS, then secure all needed state and local business licenses, professional licenses, sales-tax and employer registrations.
Open a dedicated partnership bank account funded by the initial capital contributions, set signature authority per the agreement, and never commingle personal and firm funds.
Set up bookkeeping that tracks income, expenses, and each partner's capital account, contributions, draws, and allocations, choosing cash or accrual method with an accountant.

Purchase insurance appropriate to the business: general liability, professional liability, property, auto, workers' compensation, umbrella, and the life and disability policies that fund the buy-sell agreement.
Calendar the compliance rhythm: quarterly estimated taxes for each partner, Form 1065 due March 15 with K-1s, annual state renewals, and a standing partner meeting with minutes.
Review the agreement, profit splits, insurance limits, and buy-sell valuation at least annually, and update them whenever a partner's role, the capital structure, or the business materially changes.
